articles.title: Truth Commission: Probe doctors who signed drug war death certificates
articles.summary: The Truth Commission wants five doctors who signed drug war death certificates investigated after alleged inconsistencies -- some bodies with gunshot wounds were deemed to have died from natural…

blocks.text: Published October 31, 2026 2:27am

The Truth Commission wants five doctors who signed drug war death certificates investigated after alleged inconsistencies — some bodies with gunshot wounds were deemed to have died from natural illnesses.
In a Friday report from Sandra Aguinaldo on What We Know So Far, the Truth Commission had 13 cases where the death certificates from the drug war contained false information.

The Truth Commission said that these bodies sustained gunshot wounds to the head and body, yet the death certificate listed illnesses such as pneumonia, heart attack, and sepsis as the causes of death.
The bodies of these 13 were exhumed and eventually analyzed by forensic pathologist Dr. Raquel Fortun.

The Truth Commission said that it will write to the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) and the Philippine Medical Association (PMA) to probe the five doctors who signed these death certificates.
The commission also plans to send these allegedly wrong death certificates to the two groups.
Families of drug war victims are also urged by the Truth Commission to come to them if their death certificates also listed a false cause of death.

“Pwede sila lumapit sa Truth Commission. May proseso kaming gagawin para ma-vet, ma-ascertain yung mga information na ganyan. Pwede sila matulungan kung paano, halimbawa, lumapit sa PRC para ma-correct nga yung record,” Commissioner Carlos Conde said.
(They can come to the Truth Commission. We have a process to vet, to ascertain information like that. We can help them, for example, on how to go to the PRC to correct the record.)

In a statement from the PRC, the agency said it took note of the Truth Commission’s call. Citing the “Professional Modernization Act of 2000”, the PRC said that Professional Regulatory Boards are allowed to investigate cases involving alleged violations by professionals.
The Truth Commission may also transmit these certificates and other pertinent documents to the PRC.

“The Commission, through the Professional Regulatory Board of Medicine, shall evaluate the available evidence to determine the appropriate action and assess whether sufficient grounds exist to proceed with the conduct of a motu proprio investigation,” the PRC said.
The Truth Commission may also file an administrative complaint before the Professional Regulatory Board of Medicine, together with the supporting evidence.

“If it is established by substantial evidence that the concerned doctors committed violations of the Professional Regulatory Law, the Code of Ethics of the Medical Profession, or other applicable laws, rules, and regulations, the Professional Regulatory Board of Medicine may impose the penalty of suspension or revocation of their certificates of registration to practice medicine in accordance with law,” the PRC said.

The PRC said that whether it acted on the basis of motu proprio or through a complaint, the investigation will follow applicable laws and rules, with respect to the rights of the concerned professionals.
At least 6,000 people were killed during former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs. Human rights groups estimate that the number could reach as high as 30,000.
Duterte has since been arrested and detained at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, where he awaits trial for crimes against humanity. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Men accused of sexually assaulting woman drugged by husband describe being invited to couple’s home
articles.summary:
Men say they made connection via online adverts and swinging website and had no idea Joanne Young had been drugged

Men accused of sexually assaulting a woman whose then husband drugged her…

blocks.text: Men accused of sexually assaulting a woman whose then husband drugged her for years and allowed her to be abused have described being invited to the couple’s home via online adverts and a swinging website.

One of those accused of assaulting Joanne Young, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, as she lay restrained and blindfolded said he was a young man “trying out things” and had no idea she was drugged.
A second said there was a large “cuckold community” of men who watched their wives having sex, claiming his encounter was “just a sex meet” and she seemed “fine”.

Philip Young, 50, has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and sexually abusing his former wife, 49, at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, over a number of years. The prosecution has said he advertised his wife online and “loaned” her out to other men.
Four other men are on trial at Winchester crown court, including Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, of Swindon, who denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in June 2016.

In police interviews read out to the jury, Sanderson-Doyle said he contacted Philip Young via Craigslist after seeing an ad in its adult section for a woman tied and blindfolded. He said he thought he had met a couple “trying to live out whatever their kink is”.

He said he went to the Youngs’ house on his motorcycle. He asked if he should take his shoes off when he arrived, but kept his balaclava on throughout. He saw there were toys in the house so assumed the couple had children.
Sanderson-Doyle, then 21, said he found Joanne Young “tied up and blindfolded” as she had been pictured in the online ad. She did not say anything but seemed awake.
The defendant said that at one point he heard her say “No” but he thought she wanted him to do something different rather than stop completely.
Sanderson-Doyle told police he started to get a “vibe she wasn’t enjoying it or was not comfortable” and left soon afterwards.
He continued: “I thought I had her consent. I didn’t know she was drugged,” adding: “I was just a young guy trying out things.” He called the encounter a “non event”.

A second man, Norman Macksoni, 48, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape in February 2017. He told police he worked as an MC and went by the username “dark stranger” on the swingers’ site where he made contact with Philip Young.

He said the site was “about couples living out fantasies” and there was a thriving “cuckold community”. Macksoni told police he had never had sex without consent and Joanne Young was “totally coherent”. He said: “It was just a sex meet and then I left.”
The defendant told officers he did not wear a condom and added: “He specifically said she didn’t like them.”

Also on trial are Richard Wilkins, 62, of Toothill, Wiltshire, who has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape and one of assault by penetration, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, of Swindon, who has pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual touching.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya
articles.summary: There is currently more irregular migration between eastern Libya and Crete, Greece. It's raising questions as to what connects people smugglers with powerful militias in eastern Libya and then in…

image.caption: A rescue of refugees in distress off the Libyan coastImage: Laurin Schmid/SOS MEDITERRANEE/picture alliance

blocks.text: This year, almost 20,000 people have already tried to make the perilous crossing from Libya in north Africa to the Greek island of Crete.
The route, which runs from the east coast of Libya to Greece, has become an increasingly significant corridor for irregular migration into Europe, Greek daily Kathimerini recently reported.
On Oct. 20 alone, Greek authorities registered 710 people in 14 boats. Hundreds more arrived the next day.

Many of the boats depart from areas around Tobruk, a port city on Libya's eastern Mediterranean coast. According to Kathimerini, migrants pay as much as $4,000 (€3,600) for the crossing, which takes around a day and a half.
This particular route is becoming more popular in part because of crackdowns on alternative passages.
After eastern Libyan armed forces acted against people smugglers heading for Italy in 2023, the smuggling networks changed their methods, using smaller boats and sailing them towards Crete instead.

blocks.caption: Libyans protest against irregular migration in front of the International Organization for Migration office in Tripoli, June 2026Image: Mahmud Turkia/AFP

blocks.text: Fuelling the conflict economy

According to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a think tank based in Switzerland, other groups have since entered the people smuggling business too, including those who previously mostly moved goods, vehicles or drugs.
Human trafficking in Libya is closely connected with what is known as the "conflict economy."

This sees armed actors gaining economic resources and political influence by controlling informal markets and transport routes. It also sees local power brokers using measures against smuggling to obtain financial or political support for themselves.
Social media's hidden role in human trafficking, smuggling

"Conflict and subsequent instability in Libya have created a fertile environment for migrant smuggling and TIP [trafficking in persons] activities to develop, in turn leading to the growth of smuggling in other locations along an established route," researchers at British think tank Chatham House wrote, after looking in depth at three different transit hubs across Libya. "This has led to an increase in the number of migrants entering Libya and the expansion of Libya's conflict economy."

"It remains the case that an entire business has developed around smuggling routes, regardless of whether that [smuggling] involves weapons, goods, people or drugs," Hager Ali, a researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, told DW.

If there are already contacts, transportation and security arrangements in place, then these can also be used for illegal activities like people trafficking, Ali said. Since 2014, Libya has been split into two. In the west, a United Nations-backed administration is based in Tripol; and in the east, in Tobruk, the second Libyan leadership is backed by former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar.

Haftar has managed to consolidate control over various armed militias, ruling with an iron fist. His sons also hold important positions. However, there are no proven links between the Haftars' networks and people smugglers on that coast.
But, as Ali explained, even the appearance of having some influence over these sectors can confer political influence.
"The more apparent control one has over this market, the greater one's influence," Ali told DW.

blocks.caption: A powerful and controversial figure in eastern Libya: Khalifa HaftarImage: Abdullah Doma/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Those Libyans who can influence, or even prevent, departures are demonstrating their importance to other actors. For example, high profile operations against the smuggling networks can serve as a sign of political legitimacy. "They present themselves as somebody who can restore order and curb migration," Ali noted.

There's also increasing geopolitical competition in the eastern Mediterranean. In late October, the Tobruk government signed a maritime agreement with Turkey, a deal that Turkey had actually originally concluded with Libya's other government in Tripoli.

Turkey previously fought Haftar-sponsored militias during the Libyan civil war, and this deal represents rapprochement between the two. It is also a way for Turkey to get what it wants in a rivalrous situation in this maritime area — Greece rejects the agreement, saying that it infringes on Greek economic rights around islands like Crete and Rhodes.

A direct link between the new agreement and rising numbers of irregular migrants in Crete is not clear. However, Ali suggested that it wouldn't be inconceivable that irregular migrants could be used as leverage in these kinds of geopolitical conflicts.
European cooperation
The European Union has been cooperating with Libyans to prevent irregular migrants from getting to Europe — despite the Libyan actors' links to armed groups and their disputed political legitimacy.

There's an obvious contradiction in that, argued Andreas Dittmann, a retired professor from Giessen University and expert on human geography and development. Such cooperation between the EU and Libyans can serve as a control on irregular migration but it also adds to the Libyans' local power.

"If those in charge in eastern Libya are actually able to influence the scale and timing of such [migrant] movements, they're demonstrating their own strategic importance to European governments," Dittmann told DW.
A report by the United Nations' International Organization for Migration, or IOM, illustrated how precarious the situation is for many migrants.

According to the report, which is based on data from May and June this year, around 950,000 migrants and refugees were registered as living in Libya. Many have only limited access to healthcare and tend not to have residence or work permits, all of which increases their dependence on informal markets as well as the risk of exploitation.
This story was originally published in German.

articles.title: Russell Brand trial: accusers have ‘nothing to gain’ and were not led by media, court told
articles.summary:
In closing speech, prosecutor says six women had ‘bravely’ come forward after realising they were not alone

Six women who have been “haunted” by their encounters with Russell Brand came…

blocks.text: Six women who have been “haunted” by their encounters with Russell Brand came forward to give evidence against him with nothing to gain and no appetite for fame, a court has heard.

The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said the women, who do not know one another, had not been compelled to make police complaints by the “magic force” of media reporting on Brand’s alleged misconduct.
In her closing speech, she told jurors at Southwark crown court that the women had “vivid recollections” and had “bravely” come forward to the tell “the truth” after realising they were not alone.
Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Karmy-Jones denied that a 2023 Dispatches documentary about Brand had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.

She said the complainants had described a similar pattern of behaviour, saying: “Six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not looked out for some form of publicity, who have not taken part in a documentary, not made claims for compensation.
“There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago.”

She said the women described how Brand’s “demeanour changed” before he assaulted them. “Listen to their accounts,” the prosecutor told the jury. “Many said he was nice and then it was like there was a personality change. A pivot. His eyes changed, he snapped from charming to frightening and nasty.
“He didn’t listen when they said no, he didn’t stop, he didn’t care, he kept pulling, pushing, tugging, thrusting. In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim.”

She said the women had given the court “specific details” about Brand’s conduct. “What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago.
“The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years,” she said.
The prosecutor also accused Brand of using “gaslighting” to “good effect” by asking some of his accusers for their telephone numbers or emails after the alleged assaults.
She said women were a “disposable commodity” to Brand and later added: “He was a defendant who was rampant in his desire to have sexual contact whenever her wished, whenever he pleased.”

Karmy-Jones described the account of the youngest witness, a fan then in her early 20s who accused the TV personality of anally raping her at his London townhouse after meeting her at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.
He cared only about his “birthright orgasm” and ignored her pleas for him to stop, the prosecutor said, adding that she was “just another number to add to his 5,000 notches which he was marking up”.
The court heard Brand had a “flavour of disdain” towards the allegations, which the prosecution suggested was “a reflection” of his “whole approach to the female species at that time”.
“Women as a whole were disposable, they didn’t matter to him. He didn’t even need to know their names. They were just a means to an end.
“As he said in a 2017 interview, they were the amusements in what he described as his playground of orgasms,” Karmy-Jones continued.
Earlier on Friday the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, gave legal directions to the jury in which he pointed out that they would have “rival arguments” to consider.

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
His barrister, Ian Winter KC, is due to deliver his closing speech on Monday.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Local devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell Burnham
articles.summary:
John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth say devolving power further is up to Holyrood and Senedd – not Westminster

Scotland and Wales’s first ministers have told Andy Burnham that decisions on…
articles.byline: Peter Walker, Bethan McKernan and Andrew Sparrow

blocks.text: Scotland and Wales’s first ministers have told Andy Burnham that decisions on local devolution rest solely with their parliaments, in response to the prime minister’s push to extend English-style regional powers across the UK.
After talks in Glasgow with John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth about localised employment and reindustrialisation powers, Downing Street characterised the talks as constructive.

However, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, criticised Swinney’s government before the summit for hoarding powers it acquired from Westminster rather than devolving them further, causing some friction.

Streeting told BBC Scotland: “One of the critiques we have … is that for the Scottish government, devolution is often about transferring power, responsibility, resources from Westminster to Holyrood and the challenge Andy Burnham is setting out is, ‘What about devolving more power also from Holyrood to local government across Scotland?’”

The Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, had also been due at the summit, but did not attend after a political row between Sinn Féin and the DUP. Burnham said it was “disappointing” she was not there.

The prime minister said he hoped to have all four UK nations moving at the same pace on devolution, particularly on efforts outlined in Wednesday’s budget to give mayors in England more powers over tax revenues.

“There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind,” the prime minister said. “I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also, crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.”
Ap Iorwerth said he had pushed Burnham on his wish to have more powers for his government.
He added: “I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd.”

Swinney’s post-talks comments took a similar line, saying he would “work constructively and collaboratively” in devolving more powers to his government, while adding that Burnham had assured him “that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour”.

Despite the emollient tone, tensions remain. Shortly before the summit, ap Iorwerth said Burnham’s first budget, which the Welsh government said amounted to a real-terms funding cut for the country, showed the prime minister was “not serious about Wales”.

Plaid Cymru, which won May’s Senedd elections, putting nationalists in office in all three of the UK’s Celtic nations for the first time, has already formally asked Burnham to give Wales the same devolved powers as Scotland.
The SNP-led government is regularly irritated by comments such as those by Streeting, characterised by one Scottish official as “lecturing us on devolution”.

Separately, Lee Waters, who was a minister in the Labour-led Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until the election in May, told the Guardian that Burnham, who was the Greater Manchester mayor before becoming PM, should not try to impose an English-style mayoral model on Wales, as “we are not comparing like with like”.
He said: “The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas.

“Transposing an English mayoral worldview on to a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.

“Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government.”

articles.title: IN PHOTOS | Celebrity Halloween costumes to inspire your spooky season
articles.summary: From pop icons and movie legends to unexpected throwbacks, celebrities are going all out for this Halloween. Here's a roundup of costumes turning the internet into one big Halloween party.

image.caption: This animated gif shows celebrities in Halloween costumes including Kim Kardashian, Cyndi Lauper, North West, Keke Palmer, Janelle Monáe and Elliot Page. (kimkardashian/Instagram, bettemiddler/Instagram, North West/TikTok, keke/Instagram, Michael Buckner/Variety/Getty Images, Santiago Felipe/Getty I

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
From pop icons and movie legends to unexpected throwbacks, celebrities are going all out for this Halloween. Here's a roundup of costumes turning the internet into one big Halloween party.
Celebrities channel pop culture icons, unforgettable movie characters and more

From pop culture icons to unforgettable movie characters, celebrities are bringing this Halloween to life with costumes that are equal parts creative, nostalgic and internet-breaking. Here are the celebrity looks everyone’s talking about:
Keke Palmer
Actor and singer Keke Palmer and her three-year-old son Leodis dressed up as pop music icons Michael and Janet Jackson from their 1995 Scream music video.
Paris Hilton

American media personality and socialite Paris Hilton shared two family Halloween costumes on Instagram. In the first, she’s Belle from Disney's Beauty and the Beast, joined by husband Carter Reum as the Beast, son Phoenix as Lumière and daughter London as Chip.
In the second, the family transforms into the ghoulish Addams Family, with Hilton as Morticia, Reum as Gomez, and their children as Wednesday and Pugsley.
Owen Thiele and Benito Skinner

Actor and podcaster Owen Thiele teamed up with Overcompensating co-star Benito Skinner for a music-inspired duo costume. Thiele dressed as British singer PinkPantheress, while Skinner channelled Swedish pop star Zara Larsson — a playful nod to the viral remix of PinkPantheress’s hit Stateside.
Mary Beth Barone and Benito Skinner
Skinner and comedian Mary Beth Barone recreated one of the internet’s most memorable talk-show moments as talk show host Ellen DeGeneres (Skinner) and actor Dakota Johnson (Barone).

The costumes nod to Johnson’s 2019 appearance on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, when DeGeneres said she hadn’t been invited to Johnson’s 30th birthday party. Johnson replied, "That’s not the truth, Ellen. You were invited"— and a producer confirmed she was, but couldn’t attend.
Elliot Page
Actors Elliot Page, left, and Julia Shiplett, pictured in New York on Wednesday, dressed as the "Busy Bee" scene from the 2000 mockumentary Best in Show.
(Santiago Felipe/Getty Images)
Lily Allen
British singer Lily Allen took a cheeky swipe at Ticketmaster, dressing up as the ticketing platform’s familiar seat map.
British singer Lily Allen dressed up as Ticketmaster's seat map. (lilyallen/Instagram)
Kim Kardashian

Pop culture icon Kim Kardashian channelled her eldest daughter, North West, with whom she shares custody with rapper Kanye West, for Halloween. She recreated North’s look with blue hair, facial jewelry, bold makeup and elaborate nails.
North West
Not to be outdone, North shared multiple Halloween looks on TikTok, including Edward Scissorhands, pictured below, virtual idol Hatsune Miku, Raven from Teen Titans and reality TV's Natalie Nunn.
(North West/TikTok)
Cyndi Lauper
Singer Cyndi Lauper performed as The Little Mermaid’s Ursula at the New York Restoration Project’s annual Hulaween gala on Oct. 23.
(bettemiddler/Instagram)
Bob the Drag Queen
Multi-media personality Bob the Drag Queen and fellow Drag Race alum Monét posted their best White Chicks impersonations, from the 2004 movie.
Janelle Monáe
Actor-singer Janelle Monáe dressed up as "The Amazing Fish-Boy" at her Wondaween Festival, held Thursday at the Santa Monica Pier, north of Los Angeles.
(Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)
Elmo
Sesame Street’s beloved red monster, Elmo, traded his signature look for a Miranda Priestly-inspired ensemble, channelling Meryl Streep’s character from The Devil Wears Prada.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. articles.title: Ian McKellen calls lifelong friend Patrick Stewart the 'most respected and beloved actor,' in moving tribute
articles.summary: Ian McKellen has shared a tribute to his lifelong friend Patrick Stewart in the wake of his death, describing him as true to Yorkshire upbringing and "a man to rely on, to admire and in my case,…

image.caption: Actors Ian McKellen, left, and Patrick Stewart, shown here attending the premiere of Star Trek: Picard in London on Jan. 15, 2020, have been friends for decades. Following Stewart's death, McKellen shared a moving tribute on Instagram, calling him the 'most respected and beloved actor of his generat

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Ian McKellen has shared a tribute to his lifelong friend Patrick Stewart in the wake of his death, describing him as true to Yorkshire upbringing and "a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love."
McKellen shared a post honouring his longtime friend and collaborator following Stewart’s death
There are few British acting duos quite as well-loved as Ian McKellen and Patrick Stewart — and as McKellen prepares to go on without his lifelong friend, he's reflecting on their journey together.

McKellen shared a lengthy tribute to Stewart on Wednesday night, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic," and saying he was true to his Yorkshire upbringing to the core.
"He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love," McKellen wrote in an Instagram post, accompanied by a photo of Stewart.

Stewart died on Wednesday at the age of 86 at his Los Angeles home after a "brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia," according to a statement shared on his Instagram Thursday.
Since then, a flood of tributes have cascaded in from friends, former co-stars and fans, all shining a light on what Stewart meant to them.

items: Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86

blocks.text: For two decades, McKellen and Stewart starred opposite each other as fated friends-turned-foes Magneto and Prof. Charles Xavier, respectively, in the X-Men film series. McKellen is now facing the red carpet of their final film together without his artistic partner. Both reprised their roles in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, set to be released in December.
Stewart and McKellen speak at the John L. Tishman Auditorium at University Center on Jan. 28, 2014, in New York City. (Ilya S. Savenok/Getty Images for SAG Foundation)
They first appeared together as the duo in the movie X-Men in 2000, but they’d known each other for years before that partnership cemented their friendship.

The two British actors, only a year apart in age, both came up in the theatre scene in London. Although they met through the Royal Shakespeare Company, McKellen wrote in his post, they weren't in the same productions. Still, they cared about each other's careers early on — McKellen said he remembered running into Stewart in the street while the latter was contemplating playing Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, which would become a career-defining role.
McKellen, at the time, thought it was a terrible idea, a risk to Stewart's stage career.
"Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," McKellen wrote.

items: 5 unforgettable Patrick Stewart performances as Jean-Luc Picard

blocks.text: McKellen praised his acting roles on the stage and on screen, and highlighted that one of Stewart’s proudest achievements was his appointment as Chancellor of Huddersfield University in Yorkshire.
Stewart and McKellen pose during a photo call for the X-Men: The Last Stand at the 59th International film festival in Cannes, southern France on May 22, 2006. (Jeff Christensen/The Associated Press)
A lifelong friendship

For decades, when someone mentioned Stewart, McKellen's name wasn’t far behind. They starred together in X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006) and X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014), performed on Broadway together in several theatrical productions in the 2010s and were close friends off-screen as well.
Stewart has previously said they first bonded while filming X-Men in 2000, when they shared adjoining trailers.

items: Remembering the legacy of actor Sir Patrick Stewart

blocks.text: "It was a simple matter of that we found we had a huge amount in common. I love him deeply," Stewart told The Hollywood Reporter in 2020.

When Stewart married jazz singer Sunny Ozell in 2013, McKellen officiated the wedding — which he announced on The Jonathan Ross Show by saying, "I’m going to marry Patrick," sparking a round of laughter.
Stewart later told The Hollywood Reporter that McKellen had gotten ordained specifically to be able to officiate his wedding to Ozell.

Stewart and McKellen arrive for the U.K. premiere of X-Men: Days of Future Past in London on May 12, 2014. They reprised their roles in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, their final film together. (Jonathan Short/Invision/The Associated Press)

The ease of friendship between them has included the occasional liplock on a red carpet. Since coming out in 1988, McKellen has been one of the most public gay figures in media, and while Stewart received praise for his open allyship over the years, he's said in the past that it wasn’t something he had to think about.

"There was never a moment where I made an intellectual choice that I would be a supporter of gay civil rights," Stewart said in an interview with The Advocate in 2015. "It was always a natural and uncomplicated choice."

He added that when the Guardian misidentified him as a gay man in a news story in 2014 and then ran a correction, he was "utterly flattered by that assumption." McKellen, he said, was the first to reach out to him about it, cheekily sending an email that said, "Congratulations!"
Tributes pour in for X-Men, Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart
In 2009, they shared the stage for a production of Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, an experience McKellen later said he enjoyed so much that he broke down in tears after it ended.

"I was heartbroken," McKellen told CBS News in a shared interview with Stewart. "And then we were going to say goodbye to each other. You were going off to do other things and I just felt I would never be as happy again."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programme
articles.summary:
Cryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income

North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.

Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.

North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.

Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.

A UN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.

The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.

The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.

blocks.caption: Stolen funds are used to fund North Korea’s military, including its nuclear weapons programme. Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.

“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.

North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.

A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.

The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and the production and trafficking of crystal meth for export in the 2000s.

The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.

The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.

Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film stars Jennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid less than their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.

The attack, by North Korea’s Lazarus Group, was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.

articles.title: Important chapter of Catholic abuse saga comes to close, as N.L. court ends restructuring proceedings
articles.summary: A five-year restructuring process has now come to a close, with the corporation controlling the Archdiocese of St. John's selling off 132 properties and raising more than $30 million to compensate…

image.caption: The Basilica of St. John the Baptist looms large over the St. John's skyline. The church's influence has waned in recent years, as it sold off properties to compensate victims of abuse in Catholic schools, parishes and orphanages. (Submitted by Dale Brow)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

A five-year restructuring process has now come to a close, with the corporation controlling the Archdiocese of St. John's selling off 132 properties and raising more than $30 million to compensate victims of abuse.
Church paid out $32.8M to victims through sale of 132 properties

The Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of St. John's (RCECSJ) has now transitioned into bankruptcy, putting an end to a restructuring process that saw more than 100 church properties sold off to compensate victims of abuse.

Lawyers for the church brought forth an application at the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador in St. John's on Friday morning, asking Justice Garrett Handrigan to approve the termination of proceedings under the Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA).
Handrigan obliged, ending a complicated process that started five years ago.

“No process will ever make right the terrible things that happened here, but I think we all played a positive role over the last five years," said Geoff Budden, lawyer for the largest contingent of the 369 claimants who came forward in the case.

Budden has been working on behalf of his clients for more than 30 years, starting with a drawn-out process that sought to hold somebody accountable for the abuses of the Christian Brothers who ran the Mount Cashel Orphanage in St. John's.

The survivors scored a landmark victory in 2020, when the province's court of appeal ruled the church was vicariously liable for the actions of the Christian Brothers. The Supreme Court of Canada declined to hear an appeal in 2021, putting an end to the lengthy legal saga.
CCAA proceedings followed, which resulted in the RCECSJ listing its assets for sale to compensate the growing number of victims who came forward with claims.
Geoffrey Spencer is lead counsel for the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of St. John's. (Terry Roberts/CBC)
Geoffrey Spencer, a lawyer for the RCECSJ, told the court on Friday that they initially expected about 100 claimants to come forward and estimated the value of their claims could top $50 million.
It turned out, they drastically underestimated.
In total, 369 people came forward and an independent evaluator pegged the total value of their claims at $121 million.

In the end, the CCAA proceedings resulted in the sale of 132 church properties for a total of $32.8 million. There are only seven properties left unsold, of which two have accepted offers but have yet to close.

The provincial government kicked in $45.8 million earlier this year to cover its liability to the claimants — many of whom were placed by government in an institution like Mount Cashel, or were abused while attending Catholic schools funded by the province.
Lawyers told the court on Friday that the total value paid out to survivors so far sits at $85.2 million.
"This is a significant recovery," Spencer said.
What happens next?

The Archdiocese of St. John's incorporated two new entities during the restructuring process — one to handle day-to-day operations of parishes and the other to manage properties retained by the church, such as cemeteries.

Handrigan's order releases those entities from the process going forward, meaning they cannot be targeted by future claims related to the RCECSJ. Spencer said that was crucial to allow the church and its parishioners to move forward without lasting worries.

The RCECSJ will also hold back $1 million to handle future claims or professional expenses that may arise. That includes legal costs associated with an appeal related to the church's insurance company, which is currently sitting with the Supreme Court of Canada.

Going forward, Spencer said, the RCECSJ will exist as a shell company with the few remaining properties unsold during the CCAA proceedings. If those properties are eventually sold, funds will flow to survivors with the assistance of a trustee.
St. John's lawyer Geoff Budden has been locked in litigation with the Catholic church and its related entities for 30 years. (Terry Roberts/CBC)
Budden thanked all the lawyers who were involved in the process, noting the efficiency of those involved over the last five years of a 30-year legal marathon.
Two survivors were in the gallery behind him on Friday morning, watching as the process finally came to a close.

“Their dignity and patience throughout this process has been acknowledged and I'd like to acknowledge it again here today," Budden said. "I've had the privilege of working with these men and, in some cases, their widows."

articles.title: Charges dropped against man arrested in mass shooting at Ohio festival that wounded 12
articles.summary:
Eljay Crisp-Carr, 20, spent five months behind bars before prosecutors asked to dismiss charges

Ohio prosecutors on Friday dropped…

blocks.text: Ohio prosecutors on Friday dropped charges against a man arrested in connection with the 6 June shooting at Toledo’s Old West End festival that injured 12 people.
Eljay Crisp-Carr, 20, had faced more than 50 felony charges stemming from the shooting, including 25 counts of attempted murder. He was released after spending about five months behind bars.
But during a hearing Friday before the judge Lori Olender of the Lucas county court of common pleas, prosecutors requested that the charges against Crisp-Carr be dismissed.
His mother, April Carr, told news outlet WKYC she was “ecstatic” about the outcome.
“I’m beyond excited because what mother wants their child to be broadcast across the world for something they didn’t do?” she said.
Crisp-Carr’s defense team believes another person involved in the shooting remains at large.

“Now we’re still concerned that there is still somebody out here who actually did do the shooting, and as far as we’re concerned, that guy might be still out here still shooting,” defense attorney Alex Bodiford told WKYC.

The local news outlet WTVG reported that attorneys for Crisp-Carr had said he was not even at the festival when the shooting occurred. Lawyers for Crisp-Carr said they had video and cellphone evidence that supported his alibi, according to WTVG.

The Lucas county prosecutor’s office issued a statement to the media Friday morning explaining its decision, noting the dismissal was without prejudice – meaning charges can be refiled if necessary – though also acknowledging that it had found evidence apparently supporting Crisp-Carr’s defense.

“Due to new and developing evidence, the state of Ohio asked the court to dismiss the charges against Eljay Crisp-Carr without prejudice, and the court granted the request,” the prosecutor’s office said. “In September 2026, the Lucas county prosecutor’s office informed Mr Crisp-Carr’s attorney of discovery that may support his defense.”
The statement also addressed the status of the investigation, saying it was ongoing.

“The Toledo Police Department continues its investigation,” the statement said. “Both the department and our office remain committed to following the evidence and getting it right, just as we are in every case. As we said after the shooting in June, we will try this case in a courtroom, not in a court of public opinion.”
Speaking with WTVG after the charges against him were dropped, Crisp-Carr said: “God is good.”
He maintained that he had always known he was innocent and believed authorities had mistaken him for someone else.
When asked whether he believed the mistaken identification came from photographs, Crisp-Carr responded: “Yes, sir. Just picking with me.”
He also said he had attempted to explain to authorities that he was not the individual shown in the photograph. “They told me I was a monster,” Crisp-Carr said. “They just incriminated me.”
The Old West End festival mass shooting erupted when a fight between rival groups apparently escalated into two people shooting at each other, although they were not among the wounded.
Hundreds of people were attending the annual festival in a historic district of Toledo, a city on the western edge of Lake Erie. Organizers canceled the event’s second day because of the shooting.

As of Friday, there had been more than 385 mass shootings in the US so far for the year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, a nonpartisan resource which defines such cases as those in which four or more victims are wounded or killed.
The US perennially has had high rates of mass shootings, prompting many to call on the federal government to implement more substantial gun control. But Congress has not implemented such measures.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte won't attend fifth ICC status conference ahead of trial
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte will not attend the fifth status conference before the start of his crimes against humanity trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30.

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published October 31, 2026 1:25am

Former President Rodrigo Duterte listens through headphones at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, The Netherlands on Tuesday, October 13, 2026 during the fourth status conference in his case. Screenshot from ICC livestream
Former President Rodrigo Duterte will not attend the fifth status conference before the start of his crimes against humanity trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30.

In a document released on Friday, Duterte's counsel, Peter Haynes, said Trial Chamber III had granted the former president's request to waive his appearance at the November 2 status conference, allowing him to be represented by his lawyers.
Duterte previously attended the third and fourth status conferences.

The fifth status conference will tackle the list of witnesses, number of hours for the prosecution's presentation of evidence, potentially exculpatory evidence, agreed facts, as well as protective measures inside the courtroom, among other matters.

Duterte has been in ICC custody since March 2025 in connection with charges over killings during his tenure as Davao City mayor and in relation to the war on drugs during his presidency. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
articles.summary: European foreign ministers refused to be pictured with Sergei Lavrov at the summit being held in Atlanta.

blocks.text: Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is present and a diplomatic source confirmed the UK was among the countries which refused to participate in the picture.
One British official said: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".
A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".
"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.
The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of mid-term elections at the start of November, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What happens when Rodrigo Duterte's ICC trial opens on Nov. 30?
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court"s (ICC) trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte for crimes against humanity will open on November 30, with judges first asking him whether he admits guilt or pleads…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: The International Criminal Court’s (ICC) trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte for crimes against humanity will open on November 30, with judges first asking him whether he admits guilt or pleads not guilty.
In a media advisory released by the ICC Public Affairs Unit Friday, the ICC has laid out how the opening of the trial will unfold.
Will former President Duterte appear in person?
Under Article 63 of the Rome Statute, an accused person “shall be present during the trial.”
The ICC’s own Duterte case page likewise says the accused is expected to be present during trial, while any questions about how Duterte participates will be decided by the judges.
So far, Duterte’s defense team has made no public filing about how he will appear before the court on November 30.

In October, the ICC Registry advised judges to publicly explain any arrangement allowing Duterte to leave and re-enter the courtroom during proceedings, warning that unexplained absences could fuel disinformation among audiences following the trial from the Philippines.
The Registry noted that Philippine media were expected to follow the proceedings “very intensively” and pay attention to the “smallest details” of Duterte’s appearance and conduct.
It also said victims and affected communities placed “paramount importance” on Duterte’s presence during the proceedings.

The Registry further said that, if Duterte does not attend in person, participation by video link from the ICC Detention Center could be considered, subject to the Chamber’s approval. It said such an arrangement would still allow Duterte to communicate privately with his lawyers.
How can the public watch the conference?
Yes. The ICC will stream the hearing on its website, Facebook account, and YouTube Channel with a 30-minute delay.
Members of the public may also attend in person, subject to limited gallery space and a first-come, first-served policy.
What’s the hearing schedule like?
The hearing will begin at 10 a.m. in The Hague (5 p.m. Philippine time). Each hearing day is divided into four one-hour sessions:
10 a.m. to 11 a.m. (5 - 6 p.m. Manila)
3 p.m. to 4 p.m. (10:00 - 11:00 p.m. Manila)
The advisory said that the courtroom schedule may be adjusted “on a case-by-case basis,” meaning the exact timing will depend on how quickly the opening phase progresses.
What happens first?
According to the ICC Public Affairs Unit media advisory, Trial Chamber III will first verify that Duterte understands the nature of the charges before asking him to enter a plea.
The judges will then ask whether the former president makes an admission of guilt or pleads not guilty.
Who gives the opening statements?
The Office of the Prosecution will speak first, followed by the Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV). The Defense may also give an opening statement if it chooses.
The prosecution has six hours total for its opening statement, while the CLRV has three hours. The statements will be delivered across the court’s four daily hearing sessions.
When will the first witness testify?
The first Prosecution witness is scheduled to start testifying following the conclusion of the opening statements, and the courtroom schedule will be adjusted on a case-by-case basis.
What charges does Duterte face?
Former President Duterte is charged with crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Rome Statute.
He faces three counts of the crimes allegedly committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population in the Philippines between 1 November 2011 and 16 March 2019:
Count 1: Murder as a crime against humanity in Davao City during his mayoral period, between 2013 and around June 2016
Count 2: Murder as a crime against humanity of ‘High-Value Targets’ in locations across the Philippines during his presidency between around July 2016 and July 2017.
Count 3: Murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity in barangay clearance operations in locations across the Philippines during his presidency between around July 2016 and September 2018.
Who are the judges?
The case is before Trial Chamber III, composed of Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou.
What happens after the prosecution case?
The hearings are scheduled to begin on 30 November 2026.
The Prosecution is currently expected to call a number of witnesses, after which the CLRVs may submit observations. The Defence will have the opportunity to present its case and call witnesses.
At the end of the trial hearings, the Trial Chamber judges will render their judgment within a reasonable period.
The judges will convict someone only if the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the charges have been proven beyond reasonable doubt.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky
articles.summary:
Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city near Kherson where people have faced months of severe shortages

People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky…

blocks.text: People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.

The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.
The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.
The localised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region allowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.

blocks.caption: Russian military personnel pass by damaged vehicles during a de-mining operation near Oleshky. Photograph: Russian Defence Ministry/Reuters

blocks.text: Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to the southern Russian city of Anapa.
“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he added.
While Ukrainian territory lies just 5km from Oleshky, evacuees will instead need to travel to Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.

“At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky,” Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post. Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.
While earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled on the convoy.

blocks.caption: The convoy carrying more than 500 evacuees from Oleshky. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.

Asked about whether she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a video showed a woman, who identified herself Anna, saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”

With about 2,000 people remaining in Oleshky, according to authorities and volunteers, people have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.

blocks.caption: People in Oleshky have endured months of food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation. Photograph: The Office Of The Commissioner For Human Rights In The Russia/EPA

blocks.text: Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.

“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in images broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”

Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city. “They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press.
“They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added.
The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides.
On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement.
Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023.

“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.

blocks.caption: Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets (centre), and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova (left), talk to journalists before the evacuation. Photograph: Office of the Ukrainian Ombudsman/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I’ve been told that ‌it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”
He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for ​such a significant duration.”

articles.title: Churchill River energy agreement with Quebec not open for renegotiation, says N.L.
articles.summary: Newfoundland and Labrador's premier says an agreement with Quebec to develop energy in Labrador is not open for renegotiation.

image.caption: Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador Tony Wakeham is seen at the AFN First Nations - First Ministers Meeting Day of Ceremony in Ottawa, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Keito Newman (The Canadian Press/Keito Newman)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
Newfoundland and Labrador's premier says an agreement with Quebec to develop energy in Labrador is not open for renegotiation.
'Let me be clear: we will not be renegotiating the deal,' says Wakeham
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 30, 2026 1:00 PM EDT | Last Updated: 29 minutes ago

Tony Wakeham said Wednesday that the Newfoundland and Labrador government had already voted in favour of the non-binding agreement, which he unveiled in August alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney and former Quebec premier Christine Frechette in St. John's.
"Let me be clear: we will not be renegotiating the deal, and will not entertain an attempt by anyone else wishing to renegotiate the deal," he said.

He made the remarks as reporters pressed him about whether final agreements would be signed before they were debated in the legislature. But there is also a new Parti Québécois government in Quebec that could ask for changes to the multibillion-dollar agreement.
Wakeham said he has not heard any rumblings about Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon wanting changes.
"I think what I'm trying to do is just outline our position," Wakeham told reporters in St. John's.

The proposal — which the government has called a definitive co-operation and implementation agreement — lays out plans for Hydro-Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro to expand the hydroelectric capacity of the Churchill River, which cuts through traditional Innu territory.
Carney has touted the proposal as "the largest clean energy investment in North American history" and his government has promised $10 billion in financing to help it along.
In a Facebook post Wednesday, the grand chief of the Innu Nation in Labrador said Innu were not included in the energy negotiations despite the agreement proposing projects on Innu land.
Jodie Ashini pointed to a social media post by Carney saying he met with Wakeham recently in Ottawa, and a public statement from Wakeham pledging to "keep engaging respectfully with the Innu Nation."
"How is meeting with the prime minister and discussing our lands and not having us at the table respectful?" she wrote.
"There is no respect from the [Newfoundland and Labrador] government right now to the Innu."
"Come to Sheshatshiu and speak with us," she added, referring to an Innu community in central Labrador where the Innu Nation has its main office.

Ashini has accused Wakeham and his government of interfering with a cultural exhibit detailing Innu history in Labrador. She says the government believes Innu arrived about 300 years ago, after the Europeans. The position erases thousands of years of Innu history, she has said.

On Wednesday, Wakeham said he would table all final energy agreements in the legislature and propose a special debate about them. He would not answer directly when reporters asked if thoseagreements would already be signed, but he was clear they would not be open for changes.

items: N.L. taps new lead negotiator for Churchill River power deal following resignation
Churchill River power contracts will be settled before they're seen by House of Assembly

blocks.text: The Parti Quebecois did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
St-Pierre Plamondon and his cabinet were sworn in last week, and Wakeham has not yet met with the new premier in person.
"It's coming," Wakeham said. "He wants to come to Newfoundland and Labrador for a meeting. He indicated that to me in our last conversation, and I'm looking forward to that."
