articles.title: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage
articles.summary: A 55-year-old dog rescue programme that has found missing hikers and children in the Canadian wilderness was axed as part of government budget cuts.

blocks.text: Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's vast and heavily wooded Banff National Park.
Another time, his canine partner led him hiking up a steep mountainside for two hours until they reached a man with a broken leg who was close to dying from hypothermia.
Now 73 and retired, Ward spent 17 years as a dog handler in the wilderness of the Canadian Rocky Mountains, work he described as gratifying.
Over the years, the rescue programme was cut back to just one person in the role, and Ward was shocked when he heard recently that Parks Canada will end the programme entirely as of this month.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is making broad funding cuts to Canada's public service, and Parks Canada announced last week that hundreds of their employees will soon be laid off.

The agency confirmed the news to the BBC, calling it a "difficult decision" to axe its sole dog handler position out of Banff National Park, one of the most rugged parts of Canada that welcomes more than four million visitors each year from around the world.
It added it is part of its efforts to modernise its law enforcement branch, and that "search and rescue operations will continue to be delivered" through other means.
Cutting this one role has stirred public outrage, with more than 5,000 people signing a petition since Tuesday to restore it.
William Stevenson, the Conservative Member of Parliament for the Banff area who started the petition, says he welcomes tighter government spending, but that this cut could harm public safety.
"How could they possibly make such a bad choice in where to cut?" he told the BBC.
The BBC has asked Parks Canada about how much the canine search and rescue programme cost to administer.
For 55 years, the government used rescue dogs in the Canadian Rocky Mountains who were trained to trace "everything", Ward said, from a small paper clip to shell casings to a human body.
After avalanches, a common winter hazard in the area, they were called upon to search for trapped hikers or skiers underneath heavy mounds of snow.
"It saves probers hours and hours of standing shoulder to shoulder and poking in the snow, and also exposing themselves to secondary avalanche hazards," Ward said.
In the summer, they helped find children who got lost, often after wandering away from their parents' campsites.
"We lost a huge public safety and staff safety resource," he said.
Other countries still rely on canines, often called "avalanche dogs", for mountain search and rescue, including Italy, external.
The last dog in Parks Canada's programme, a German Shephard named Leroy, was retired in August.
For the seven years that he was on the job, Leroy helped track 156 people, find 57 who were lost in the wilderness, and solve two murders in Banff.

A new canine was trained and ready for duty before Parks Canada gave notice last week that the programme would be eliminated as part of recent C$145m ($104m; £78m) budget cuts to Parks Canada, local newspaper Rocky Mountain Outlook reported.
Along with his petition, Stevenson also raised the issue in Canada's parliament during a late sitting on Thursday.

In response, Ryan Turnball, a Liberal MP and the parliamentary secretary for finance, said the government is focused on reducing Canada's deficit and "ensuring public funds support growth, resilience and the well-being of Canadians".
Stevenson said he will continue to push on the issue, and has asked for a sit-down meeting with Parks Canada's CEO.
As for Ward, he hopes that the programme will soon be restored.

He recalled a quote that was often uttered by an old park warden who trained him: "You can make an armpit smell like a lilac bush and you can put a man on the moon, but nothing can replace the nose of the avalanche dog."

articles.title: PITX: Bicol-bound bus trips continue despite Mayon eruption
articles.summary: Despite Mayon Volcano's eruption on Friday morning, bus trips bound for Bicol from the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) remain uninterrupted.

blocks.text: Published October 31, 2026 12:51am
Despite Mayon Volcano's eruption on Friday morning, bus trips bound for Bicol from the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) remain uninterrupted.

In a "24 Oras" report by Jonathan Andal, PITX said six out of every 10 buses bound for Bicol were already fully booked. However, walk-in passengers could still be accommodated on ordinary and air-conditioned buses with available seats.
While some Bicol-bound passengers expressed concern over Mayon's eruption, they still pushed through with their trips. Others, meanwhile, were unaware of the volcanic activity.
“Nakakapagalala kasi wala po kaming balita talaga na pumutok pala yung bulkan. Hangga’t mayroon pong bumabyahe, parang tutuloy po kami,” said Daisy Belga, a passenger bound for Albay.
(It's worrying because we had no idea that the volcano had erupted. But as long as buses are still operating, we will push through with our trip.)
“Kinakabahan, pero mostly kasi tagilid naman kami, [sa] Polangui. Medyo gilid man pero abot kami ng ashfall,” added Virgie Magalona, another passenger bound for Albay.
(I'm nervous, but we're somewhat off to the side in Polangui. Even though we're not directly in the affected area, ashfall can still reach us.)
In Andal's report, a bus company said its drivers traveling to Bicol had reported no problems along their routes. However, driver Lito Rodriguez said he would remain cautious.
“Medyo delikado. Magpapa-ano na lang, magpapababa muna ng abo,” Rodriguez said.
(It's somewhat dangerous. I'll just wait for the ash to settle first.)
PITX said buses with online reservation systems were already fully booked, but many buses without online booking options continued to operate even without full passenger loads.
Since October 25, PITX has recorded more than one million passengers.
The terminal's security personnel have also confiscated hundreds of prohibited items, including pointed objects and flammable materials.
Passengers heading to their hometowns brought various types of luggage, with some even traveling with their pets.
PITX said pets are generally allowed on buses with their owners, provided they comply with the requirements.
“Usually ina-allow ng mga buses natin. Dapat po may cage, vaccination card at siyempre diaper po,” PITX Deputy Spokesperson Kolyn Gervacio-Calbasa said.
(Our buses generally allow pets, provided they are in cages and have vaccination cards and diapers.)
Meanwhile, large crowds of passengers have also started gathering at the Five Star bus terminal in Cubao, Quezon City, with some trips bound for Cagayan already fully booked.

Victory Liner has increased its trips to Baguio to 250 from the previous 150, as it expects passenger volume on the route to double to 10,000 starting October 31, 2026. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Tennessee woman Christa Pike describes pain after failed execution
articles.summary: Christa Pike says she remains in constant pain a month after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee. Her lawyers want her death sentence reduced to life, while the state governor has ordered an…

image.caption: Pike was convicted of murdering her classmate (FILE: 04/12/2007)Image: J. Miles Cary/Knoxville News Sentinel/USA TODAY NETWORK/REUTERS

blocks.text: Death row inmate Christa Pike said Friday that she remained in constant pain and struggled to speak a month after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee.
Her lawyers have urged Governor Bill Lee to reduce her death sentence to life imprisonment, but he has indicated that it will remain unchanged unless the courts intervene.
In her first public statement since the failed execution, Pike said she had expected to die but instead woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said. "My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak."
What happened during the execution attempt?

Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital during the September 30 execution attempt. Her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered. She spent the first few days in hospital unconscious and on a ventilator.
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the intravenous line caused the drug to collect in surrounding tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.
Newly released 911 calls reveal chaotic response to save Christa Pike
Lee ordered an investigation and postponed Tennessee's other lethal injection scheduled this year. The state's prison chief resigned.
What did Pike say?
Pike blamed the failed execution on "incompetence" and said her suffering extended beyond her physical injuries.
"There is pain in my mind and in my soul," she said.
She also expressed gratitude to the medical workers who saved her life and acknowledged the suffering of her victim's family.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and killing of her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time of the crime, which she committed with her boyfriend.
"I continue to think about my victim's family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured," she said.
What happens next?
Lee told reporters this week: "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts."
Pike dictated her statement to her legal team from the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she returned after hospitalization.
"I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next," she said. "For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time."

articles.title: BP profits hit ‘obscene’ 18-year high as Iran war drives up oil refining margins
articles.summary:
Oil giant comes under fire from climate campaigners, as its earnings reach $8.46bn while ‘innocent civilians suffer’

BP’s quarterly profits have been labelled “obscene” after they hit an…
articles.byline: Jillian Ambrose, Damien Gayle and Lauren Almeida

blocks.text: BP’s quarterly profits have been labelled “obscene” after they hit an 18-year high of $8.46bn (£6.3bn), as the war in the Middle East drove up oil and gas prices.

The energy company hailed a “banner quarter” on Friday, with its underlying ​replacement ⁠cost profit – a key measure of its income – almost quadrupling in the three months to the end of September, from $2.2bn in the same period ​a year ​ago. The jump meant BP’s quarterly profits hit their highest level since the $8.9bn recorded in 2008.

BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill, told Bloomberg TV: “It really was a banner quarter for the refining business. We had very strong margins from the BP-operated refineries, we also had very strong underlying performance. We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market.”
However, climate crisis campaigners said it was outrageous that BP was profiting so handsomely on commodities causing serious damage to the environment.

It is just over a week until diplomats will meet in Antalya, Turkey, for the Cop31 UN climate summit. Recent climate-linked disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal will be at the forefront of many delegates’ minds. There are likely to be tensions with fossil fuel producing countries, which have sought to stymie calls for a transition to clean energy.

BP’s strong results also come as motorists in the UK face high fuel prices, with diesel now at 198.79p a litre, according to estimates from the RAC. The cost of petrol has also risen, with an average price of 172.92p a litre, compared with 132.83p in late February, before the latest conflict in the Middle East began.

Jonathan Noronha-Gant, of the campaign group Global Witness, said it was “obscene that polluters are continuing to cash in on the fallout of the war in Iran, making more bumper profits from spiralling oil prices while innocent civilians suffer.
“These massive profits come as ordinary people across Europe are struggling with the rising cost of living, with many struggling to afford to heat their homes as winter arrives,” he said.

Danny Gross, of Friends of the Earth, said: “As millions of households brace themselves for a cold winter, huddling under blankets and clutching hot-water bottles as they struggle to pay their bills, BP is raking in huge profits while doubling down on gas and oil production and slashing investment in renewables.”

Although the link between fossil fuels and climate breakdown has been known for decades, scientists directly linked carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel companies to dozens of deadly heatwaves for the first time a year ago. Yet more heatwaves swept across Europe this summer, with separate research suggesting they led to a record 50,000 excess deaths.

As people in cities sweltered, infernos tore through forests and brush in parched rural areas. France experienced its largest area burned on record and fires blazed in usually cooler regions, such as the Cairngorms in Scotland.

In the Pacific, a supercharged El Niño is brewing, with water temperatures reaching more than 3C higher than usual. The weather phenomenon is likely to be the most extreme of its kind in at least 1,000 years, dumping vast amounts of extra heat into an atmosphere already warmed by climate breakdown.

“The climate crisis is not an abstract future threat,” said Clémence Dubois, head of global campaigns at 350.org. “People are facing deadly heat, destroyed livelihoods and growing insecurity now. Governments are being forced to find money to protect their populations, while fossil fuel companies are forecast to make extraordinary profits.”
after newsletter promotion

Record oil company profits come as the UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is weighing up whether to allow drilling in the North Sea’s Rosebank oilfield, after approving a licence for the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield earlier in October.

BP’s quarterly earnings were bolstered by higher profits from the oil refining business as the difference between the cost of crude oil and the price of refined fuels such as diesel and gasoline soared, earning almost $47 for each barrel produced.

Although global oil prices have remained below the peaks recorded during the 2022 energy crisis, the pump prices for fuels, including diesel, have risen to all-time highs across the UK, Europe and the US in recent months because of severe disruptions to refineries in the Gulf region and across Russia.

BP’s earnings windfall announcement came after Shell and the French oil rival TotalEnergies reported their strongest profits since 2022, also thanks in large part to the profits made from refining crude into fuel products such as diesel.

articles.title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
articles.summary: The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.

blocks.text: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.

The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.

America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.
The company also told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
Binance had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.

But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.

In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

articles.title: What the rift within the Tsikhanouski family means for the Belarusian opposition in exile
articles.summary: Siarhei Tsikhanouski criticizes the work of his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, and her office. He also questions her legitimacy. What are the implications for Belarusian political forces in exile?

image.caption: Siarhei Tsikhanouski and his wife Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya in the European parliament in October 2025Image: Philipp von Ditfurth/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Blogger and dissident Siarhei Tsikhanouski , 48, was detained in Belarus in May 2020, after he had announced to challenge the country's ruler, Alexander Lukashenko, in the upcoming presidential elections. In December 2021, Tsikhanouski was convicted to 18 years in prison, in part for organizing "mass unrest."

After his arrest his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, took his place and challenged Lukashenko as presidential candidate. Despite allegations of large-scale vote-rigging, Lukashenko was declared the winner of the election in August 2020. This triggered unprecedented mass protests across the country. They were violently suppressed, and thousands of government critics were arrested or fled into exile. Tsikhanouskaya also fled her homeland and became the leading representative of the Belarusian democratic movement.
In June 2025, Siarhei Tsikhanouski was released after nearly five years in prison and was forcibly taken out of the country.
Blogger in exile

Some 14 months after his release, the blogger has re-activated his YouTube channel, where he not only denounces Alexander Lukashenko's regime, but also Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's office, Belarusian media in exile, political analysts and others. Thousands of people follow his streams.

In one of them, Tsikhanouski claims that while Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya obviously enjoyed "a certain legitimacy from the European Union," the people who were living "quietly and silently" in Belarus today had not granted her any. He said that many of those who had voted for her as joint candidate of Belarus' opposition were regretting this today.
What does Tsikhanouski propose?

Tsikhanouski has suggested that a supervisory board should be established under the label "United Office of Demoratic Forces." It would be made up of "former presidential candidates, protest leaders and iconic figures of the revolution," including himself and his wife. "There would not be a full legitimacy but one which was at least granted by Belarusians," Tsikhanouski said, adding that such a supervisory board could oversee the distribution of grant funds.

blocks.caption: Speaking in the Czech senate in 2021, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya holds up a photo of her husbandImage: Vondrou Roman/CTK/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Speaking about his wife, he said: "Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya was a so-called technical candidate, who received the votes of all those who were against Lukashenko. The percentage of votes she received in the 2020 election was negligible because no one knew who she was. She was allowed to run because she did not pose a threat for the regime, and because she had neither supporters nor political experience."
What's happening in the Tsikhanouski family?

Asked by DW what his goals were, Siarhei Tsikhanouski refused to comment and referred to his livestreams instead. The former political prisoner is residing in the US and is, by his own account, currently unemployed. At the beginning of summer he said he was living in Los Angeles, learning English, preparing for university studies and writing a book. It is also known that his children — a teenage son and a younger daughter — temporarily stayed with him in the US. Today, however, they attend school in Poland, where Tsikhanouskaya resides.

Neither she nor her office have commented on the family situation or her husband's allegations. Even before the public dispute, the leader of the Belarusian democratic forces avoided commenting on her husband. Asked about his activities, she often suggested to approach him directly.

Speaking to DW in December 2025, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya merely said: "What happens in the public sphere and what happens at home, are different things. I understand Siarhei's deep traumatization and also his very strong reactions to certain events. Siarhei was in prison for five years, and I look at it with great understanding. This is why I'm not going public or making any comments. We'll deal with it among ourselves."
Democratic forces in a leadership crisis?

During the 32-year-long rule of the Lukashenko regime, the Belarusian opposition has weathered many crises and conflicts. Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's leadership role has been called into question more than once. However, she and her team have always managed to work themselves out of difficult situations during the last couple of years. But will she still be able to do that now, with her own husband having turned into her critic?

Siarhei Tsikhanouski had gone back to his own self, said political scientist Yury Drakakhrust: "With all his idiosyncrasies, his style of debate, which is not exactly in line with common practice. This is likely to strike many as odd, including Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's international partners."

Tsikhanouski, Drakakhrust pointed out, insisted that he was the key figure of the 2020 events, which is why he was entitled to all the benefits, privileges, recognition and invitations. But there was no way back.

"Even if we assume that Tsikhanouski is right, that he was the central figure, what good would it do today?" he asked. "If, suddenly, hundreds of thousands of Belarusians watched his livestreams, collected funds, formed local groups or associations in Tsikhanouski's name, then perhaps it would be possible to turn back the wheel. But this will hardly be the case."

blocks.caption: Siarhei Tsikhanouski and Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya at a rally organized by Belarusian diaspora in Warsaw in June 2025Image: Czarek Sokolowski/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Drakakhrust described the current situation within the democratic forces as a "crisis." He doubted that Tsikhanouski would be able to reach an agreement with all the members of the supervisory board he has proposed. Furthermore, his wife, in particular, had since established certain assets, resources, and a status for herself through her office.
Tsikhanouskaya — recognized beyond Belarusian borders

"Tsikhanouskaya is being received at high levels, if not as an elected president, then as a leader for Belarus and Belarusian democracy. She's not regarded as just one of several democratic leaders from Belarus," the political scientist said.

He pointed out that not only Tsikhanouskaya, but also other actors from the 2020 election campaign are in exile. They, however, had not achieved a similar level of representation or comparable access to resources. "She has surpassed them as a politician, and that's what counts."

Drakakhrust said that the Belarusian government views disputes among the opposition with a touch of irony, occasionally adding fuel to the fire: "Basically, they don't care who wins. The main thing is that there is conflict, bickering and mutual vilification."
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’
articles.summary: Binance exchange says it will cover customer losses as it scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far

blocks.text: The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.
Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars.

Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.
Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets.

The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who was jailed for four months in 2024 after pleading guilty to money laundering violations. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”

blocks.caption: Binance was founded by Changpeng Zhao. Photograph: Anthony Kwan/Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.
In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.”

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.

North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.
Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the FBI and the US Secret Service.
after newsletter promotion

Tether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m. The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic.

blocks.caption: Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance: ‘Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.’ Photograph: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg/Getty

blocks.text: World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers.
Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.
Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.

The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.

A spokesperson for the FCA said: “While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in the UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.”
The Bank of England is also monitoring the hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there are no active concerns. The Bank declined to comment.
Coinbase, another major cryptocurrency exchange, said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.

In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, the prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: Canada faces fresh scrutiny, calls to do more to prevent Canadian corporate abuses abroad
articles.summary: Human rights advocates are renewing their calls for Canada to put forward "binding laws" and set up an independent mechanism to investigate possible abuses linked to the activities of Canadian…

image.caption: A Canadian flag flies on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Aug. 22. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics

Human rights advocates are renewing their calls for Canada to put forward "binding laws" and set up an independent mechanism to investigate possible abuses linked to the activities of Canadian companies outside the country.
Advocates say government must put forward 'binding laws' to curb possible abuses
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 30, 2026 12:21 PM EDT | Last Updated: 39 minutes ago

Canada is under renewed pressure to hold Canadian companies accountable for alleged human rights and environmental abuses abroad, months after the government announced it was shuttering a corporate watchdog office that investigated wrongdoing.
The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) held a hearing Tuesday in Panama to examine how Canadian extractive industries have impacted communities across the Americas region.
A day later, human rights advocates spoke at a news conference in Ottawa to demand more action from the federal government to address the issue.

items: Corporate watchdog was still accepting complaints as Carney abruptly closed it down

blocks.text: "Companies waving the Canadian flag are profiting from human rights abuse and environmental destruction," Aidan Gilchrist-Blackwood, co-ordinator of the Canadian Network for Corporate Accountability, told reporters on Wednesday.
"We're here saying enough is enough."
Long-standing concerns

The federal government has faced calls for years to do more to prevent abuses linked to Canadian companies operating outside the country. That includes Canadian firms that have been accused of being tied to threats and violence against local community members, as well as environmental harms.

But this week's push comes at a critical time, advocates say, as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government prioritizes new international trade ties — and it also recently announced the closure of the Office of the Canadian Ombudsperson for Responsible Enterprise (CORE).
Prime Minister Mark Carney, pictured in the House of Commons on Wednesday, said in June that his government had closed the CORE office. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
Established in 2019 under then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, CORE had been charged with investigating alleged abuses linked to the mining, oil and gas, and garment sectors.

But Carney raised apparent concerns with its efficiency on June 11, saying the office only launched one investigation in seven years. "Part of government is to look at things and see whether or not they're effective and try to improve it," he told reporters.

While rights groups and opposition lawmakers also had criticized CORE's lack of effectiveness, they blamed the Liberal government for failing to give the office teeth and argued it should have been strengthened, not dismantled.

items: Canada 'turning its back' on holding companies accountable for rights violations, advocates say

blocks.text: "The decision to close the CORE is a betrayal of Canada's stated commitment to human rights, corporate accountability and communities around the world that have suffered harm," NDP MP Heather McPherson said during Wednesday's news conference in Ottawa.

"The government dismantled one of the few avenues available to marginalized people, workers, Indigenous communities and human rights defenders who are seeking accountability from Canadian corporations operating overseas."
National Contact Point
The federal government has said another office, called the National Contact Point (NCP), will handle complaints about Canadian firms' operations abroad.

The NCP "aims to support early resolution, prevent escalation and strengthen corporate due diligence," Gillian Gillen, Canada's interim representative at the Organization of American States, said during Tuesday's IACHR hearing in Panama.
"Its value lies in accessibility and flexibility, and its ability to foster open, constructive and solutions-oriented dialogue between the parties without requiring litigation."

Ben Chalmers, senior vice-president of the Mining Association of Canada, said that, given the limited use of the CORE, "it makes sense to just have a single mechanism [the NCP] that can deal with all industries."
Canada to tighten forced labour import bans after Trump tariff threat
Chalmers also said Canadian courts are the "more suitable mechanism" if groups want to be able to get subpoenas and compel evidence and testimonies.
"Our view is that the NCP and the CORE, until it was folded into the NCP, were a complementary mechanism to what Canada has already established in terms of judicial mechanisms," he told CBC News.
Rights advocates say that while courts in Canada have heard cases related to corporate abuses abroad before, accessing the Canadian legal system remains difficult.
Forced labour legislation

Separately, Gillen said Ottawa has taken action on forced labour, pointing to a 2024 federal law that requires specific entities and institutions to report annually on steps taken to prevent the risk of forced and child labour in their supply chains.

Earlier this year, after the U.S. announced plans to impose sanctions on Canada and dozens of other countries over allegations they allowed forced labour into their supply chains, the Liberal government also introduced new legislation to address the issue.

items: Trump hits Canada, nearly 60 other nations with tariffs based on ‘forced labour’
25 states sue Trump administration over forced labour tariffs

blocks.text: Tabled this month in the House of Commons, Bill C-35 would authorize Canada's minister of foreign affairs to draft a list of goods for which there are "reasonable grounds" to suspect they are made with forced labour.
Anyone wishing to import those goods would then have to provide information to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), upon request, to show forced labour wasn't used.
Canada "remains committed to respecting human rights and promoting responsible business conduct abroad through prevention, legislation and mechanism for remedy," Gillen said Tuesday.
'We need binding laws'
But critics like Gilchrist-Blackwood, at the Canadian Network for Corporate Accountability, say the government's measures don't go far enough.

Noting that the National Contact Point is a "voluntary mechanism that can only promote dialogue," he said Ottawa has failed to make its expectations that Canadian companies respect human rights abroad enforceable.
"We need binding laws … [and] we need a credible and independent mechanism to investigate abuses," Gilchrist-Blackwood said this week. "Canadians continue to call on our government to act."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.

articles.title: FDA again bypasses advisers to remove black-box warnings from menopause treatments
articles.summary:
Some experts express concern about ‘lack of transparency’ as agency removes warnings on three estrogen patches

Three more patches for treating menopause will no longer carry black-box…

blocks.text: Three more patches for treating menopause will no longer carry black-box warnings about cardiovascular disease, breast cancer and dementia, officials at the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said on Friday.

The FDA did not convene an advisory committee and offered few details on the scientific basis for the decision in the press briefing. The news follows the removal of black-box warnings from six menopause treatments in February, as patients across the US struggle with shortages of the patches.
When journalists asked for the evidence behind this decision, officials said it could be provided later.

“I have been concerned by the lack of transparency behind these decisions,” said Reshma Ramachandran, an assistant professor and health services researcher at Yale School of Medicine. “The blanket removal of black-box warnings regarding risks of breast cancer and cardiovascular disease without clear justification can be misleading for patients and underplays real potential harms.”

There are particular risks for certain groups of patients, such as those with histories of hormone-sensitive cancers, she said. Instead, officials highlighted the shortages patients are facing for menopause hormone treatments (MHT).

“We are working with manufacturers to strengthen supply and improve access,” said Dorothy Fink, deputy director of the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development. Manufacturing of estrogen patches has doubled over the past year, she said.
Even so, patients report stock-outs of the patches.

“We know that for some patients, these past months have been frustrating,” said Sarah Ibrahim, deputy center director for regulatory programs of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. After the change to labels in February, demand for estradiol patches “increased significantly, and patients in many areas found it difficult to get their usual patches at their usual pharmacy”, she said. “And I want you to know that we hear you.”
The FDA is working with manufacturers to ramp up production, and the agency is also working to change the labels of the remaining MHT products, Ibrahim said.

The black-box warnings “painted a broad and, in some cases, overstated pictures of risk”, she said. “Updated evidence shows that for many healthy women under 60 and within 10 years of menopause onset, the risk-benefit profile looks meaningfully different than older warnings conveyed.”

Estradiol patches are usually considered lower risk than synthetic oral medications, because they pass into the bloodstream without first going to the liver. The risks of the patches are higher with high doses, research shows.

Officials in the Trump administration have made sweeping and “data-free” claims about the benefits of MHT, including improvements in longevity, which are not supported by research, menopause experts have said. While there are benefits to the treatments for some women, the decision not to convene advisers or include research sets a troubling precedent, they said.

The FDA bypassed its advisory committees last November in announcing it would remove the warnings; at the time, a spokesperson said that the reason is because committees are “bureaucratic, long, often conflicted, and very expensive”.

Instead, the FDA convened a panel in July 2025 featuring doctors and influencers, all of whom were vocal proponents of MHT and several of whom had conflicts of interest with practices that market and sell hormone therapy, Ramachandran said.

“At the expert meeting, they also did not allow for public testimony,” Ramachandran said – including from the lead investigator of the Women’s Health Initiative, research from which formed the recommendations for MHT, who was in the audience. After audience members voiced concern, the FDA opened a docket for public comment.
The FDA is also exploring the possibility of offering vaginal estrogen products over the counter, according to an agency press release on Friday.

articles.title: US midterms: Pope Leo XIV casts vote by mail
articles.summary: As a US citizen, Pope Leo XIV is eligible to vote in US elections and has made use of that right with a postal ballot ahead of Tuesday's midterms. The pontiff, a Chicago native, did not reveal who he…

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV is a politically outspoken pontiff and has criticized US President Donald TrumpImage: Ciro De Luca/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV has become the first ever pontiff to vote in a United States general election after submitting a mail-in ballot ahead of November's midterms, the Vatican confirmed on Friday.
The 71-year-old US citizen, who was born in Chicago, Illinois, as Robert Francis Prevost, applied for a postal vote on October 3, according to US media.
The Holy See's press office said in a statement that the pope "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen" and has done so "whenever he was eligible to do so."
Indeed, records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections show that Robert Prevost has voted in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022, including five primary elections.
Through his time as a bishop in Peru, Pope Leo also holds Peruvian citizenship and the Vatican said he had also voted whenever eligible while living in the South American country.

"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," said a spokesperson in Vatican City, which itself is an absolute monarchy and does not hold political elections.
Pope Leo XIV. warns of 'new senseless slaughter' in Europe
Pope Leo XIV: Do we know who the pontiff voted for?
In Tuesday's US midterm elections, all seats in the House of Representatives and about one third of the Senate are set to be contested.
US President Donald Trump's Republicans are seeking to defend narrow majorities in both chambers against a strong challenge from the Democrats.
In Illinois, voters are deciding whether to elect Governor JB Pritzker for a third term, and are also filling an open US Senate seat after the retirement of longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin.
It remains unclear who Pope Leo has voted for but the pontiff has repeatedly clashed with President Trump and his administration since the start of his pontificate a year and a half ago.
Leo has criticized Trump on issues such as the Iran war, migration and press freedom and declined an invitation to the United States' 250th anniversary celebrations earlier this year.
The two are yet to meet personally but Trump has often attacked the pontiff personally, calling him "weak" and captive to the "radical left."
"I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for," Leo responded while on a trip to Algeria in April.
"I will continue to speak out strongly against war, seeking to promote peace, promoting dialogue and multilateralism among states to find solutions to problems."
Can Pope Leo move President Trump on the Iran war?

articles.title: ‘Blood has no religion:’ Moro leaders demand end to Middle East violence
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — Declaring that “innocent blood has no religion,” two prominent Moro leaders in Mindanao are demanding universal accountability and an immediate end to the escalating military…

Invoking a Quranic verse on human dignity, Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) acting chairman Shaykh Abdulkarim Tan Misuari called attention to the sanctity of human life, reminding the global community that compassion and justice must remain universal. articles.title: Pope Leo votes in US midterms in first known political ballot for any pontiff
articles.summary:
US citizen Leo, who has clashed with Donald Trump over several issues, submits his vote by post in Chicago

Pope Leo has voted in the US midterm elections – the first time a pontiff is known…

blocks.text: Pope Leo has voted in the US midterm elections – the first time a sitting pontiff is known to have cast a ballot in any political election at any time in history.

Leo, who has clashed with the US president, Donald Trump, over several issues, submitted his vote by post in Chicago, where he was born, the Vatican said on Friday. Leo became the first American leader of the Catholic church last year after the death of Pope Francis.

The Vatican said Leo “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so”, including in Peru, where he lived for years as a missionary. “The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” the statement added.
Leo, who before being elected pope was known as Robert Prevost, reportedly made his request for the mail-in ballot on 3 October, registering at an address in New Lenox, Illinois.
That was 10 days before he had surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. The pontiff has gradually been resuming activities since being discharged from hospital on 17 October.
The crucial midterm elections are due to be held on 3 November.
Leo and Trump have clashed over the US president’s harsh immigration polices, with the pontiff describing them as “inhuman”.

Earlier this year, Trump lashed out in response to Leo’s criticisms of the US-Israeli war on Iran, calling the pontiff “weak on crime” and “terrible on foreign policy”. The US president also said Leo had only been elected pope because Trump himself was in the White House.
In response to the tirade, Leo said he was “not afraid” of Trump.

In his first key address to the US on the eve of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, Leo praised the country’s history of ⁠welcoming migrants, while urging Americans to live up to the ideals put forward in the ⁠declaration, in what was seen a further rebuke to Trump.

In an interview with the US broadcaster in late July, Leo expressed “great love” for his home country and its core principles of freedom, opportunity and welcoming immigrants but qualified that he just “happens to be American”.

Leo will travel to Latin America in November for an 11-day trip covering 10 cities. Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, told reporters at Rome’s foreign press association this week that a papal visit to the US was expected in the “not too distant future”, adding that the outcome of the midterms might influence whether the trip went ahead in 2027 or later.
