articles.title: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on Trump military aid decision
articles.summary: Chris Murphy said waiving a human rights condition on aid paved the way for arrests of journalists.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
US Senator Chris Murphy
ByTom Bateman
State department correspondent
A top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.

Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.

Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.
The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".
Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked.
"The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.
On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Madr Masa and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".
Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.

Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.

blocks.caption: Image caption, US President Donald Trump at a meeting with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump at a meeting with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi
Washington sends Egypt £1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.

US law allows up to £320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.

In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.

Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.

Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".
It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Six journalists from the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh who were arrested in Egypt and are facing terrorism charges

blocks.text: Image source, Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights
Six journalists from the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh who were arrested in Egypt and are facing terrorism charges

Rubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza.
Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.
Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue.

"To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI.
"Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.

US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Amnesty International called the verdict against Lina Attalah 'a crushing blow to press freedom' (file photo)

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Amnesty International called the verdict against Lina Attalah 'a crushing blow to press freedom' (file photo)
The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt, external as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.

The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Madr Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.
He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country.
"It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC.
"Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."
He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

articles.title: Akbayan's Cendaña invokes free speech in seeking dismissal of Quiboloy libel complaint
articles.summary: Akbayan party-list Representative Percy Cendaña on Friday asked the Pasig Office of the City Prosecutor to dismiss the libel and cyber libel complaint filed against him by detained religious leader…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 11:07pm

Akbayan party-list Representative Percy Cendaña on Friday asked the Pasig Office of the City Prosecutor to dismiss the libel and cyber libel complaint filed against him by detained religious leader Apollo Quiboloy.

In his counter-affidavit, Cendaña argued that his remarks during a radio interview, which Quiboloy cited in his complaint, are protected by the constitutional right to freedom of expression and constitute fair comment.

He said his statements were made in the context of the criminal cases Quiboloy faces in the Philippines and the United States, including charges of qualified human trafficking, child abuse, and sex trafficking.
Among the statements Cendaña made during the interview that Quiboloy cited in his complaint were:

“Kaya pa rin niyang manakot nung kanyang mga naging biktima while he is incarcerated.”(He can still intimidate his victims while he is incarcerated.)“Nakita naman natin kung papaano isa-isa yung mga witnesses tinatakot at hinaharass nila para bumaligtad, no? At kahit yung mga biktima, tinakot at hinarass nila para hindi ituloy ang laban.”(We have seen how witnesses were threatened and harassed to change their statements. Even the victims were threatened and harassed to discourage them from pursuing their cases.)“Hindi ito ano, hindi simpleng misconduct lamang. Ito ay ano, talagang malala na heinous crime, pag pinag-usapan natin yung sexual exploitation na mga... sexual abuse ng mga minors.”(This is not simple misconduct. These are serious, heinous crimes, particularly when we talk about the sexual exploitation and sexual abuse of minors.)“Pero sa tingin ko napakalaking bagay para sa kanila at sa kanilang mga pamilya na itong si Quiboloy ay masabi na guilty doon sa napakaraming krimen na ginawa niya mismo sa mga kasama niya sa kanyang relihiyon o simbahan, at ganun din doon sa mga kababayan natin na inaabuso niya dito ng sex trafficking, fraud at coercion.”(But I think it would mean a great deal to them and their families for Quiboloy to be found guilty of the numerous crimes he allegedly committed against members of his religion or church, as well as against fellow Filipinos who were subjected to sex trafficking, fraud, and coercion.)
Cendaña cited Article III, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution, which protects freedom of speech and expression.

"This protection assumes particular importance when the subject of the speech concerns criminal justice, government investigations, the activities of influential public personalities, and the conduct of public affairs. The complainant has not established the elements necessary to bring my statements outside the protection afforded to good faith public commentary under the Constitution and applicable jurisprudence," Cendaña said.

He also argued that his statements, when read in the context of the entire interview, were not defamatory because they did not directly accuse Quiboloy of being guilty of the crimes charged against him.

“Hence, the claim of the complainant that the statements 'state(s) the conclusion, without termination of my trial, that I have heinously abused or victimized women' are erroneous interpretation of the aforementioned statements,” Cendaña said.
Cendaña said that his remarks were "made with good motives and for justifiable ends."
"It is not equivalent to a judicial declaration of guilt," he said.
GMA News Online has reached out to Quiboloy's counsel, Ferdinand Topacio, for comment. This story will be updated once his response becomes available. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe
articles.summary:
Archaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79

Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to…

blocks.text: Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii.

The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii.
The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern.

blocks.caption: A charm from a crepundia, a type of necklace often worn by children. Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological Park

blocks.text: But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury.
The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified.
“A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.

“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.”
The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson.
The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said.
Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home.

blocks.caption: Bronze weights and a box closure found among the possessions. Photograph: SV_POMPEII/via Pompeii Archaeological Park

blocks.text: The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its ​facade was first excavated ​in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.
There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century.

blocks.caption: A bronze oil lamp with a deflector. Photograph: SV_POMPEII/via Pompeii Archaeological Park

blocks.text: “It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters.

“So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.”

Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city.
A home containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.

articles.title: Who counts as a victim in Rodrigo Duterte trial? ICC Registry asks Trial Chamber's guidance
articles.summary: The Victims Participation and Reparation Section (VPRS) of the International Criminal Court (ICC) Registry is asking Trial Chamber III for guidance on reassessing the applications of drug war…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: PRAGUE, Czech Republic – The Victims Participation and Reparation Section (VPRS) of the International Criminal Court (ICC) Registry is asking Trial Chamber III for guidance on reassessing the applications of drug war victims, following the approved scope of the case against former President Rodrigo Duterte.

In a public redacted report dated October 29, the VPRS said at least 13 of 251 applications previously authorized during the pre-trial phase, representing 16 of 539 victims who will participate in the trial, now appear to fall outside the case’s scope.

It may be recalled that Trial Chamber III previously decided to apply “temporal parameters” to the confirmed charges against Duterte, which led to the removal of Incident 57 that the Office of the Prosecutor had applied for.

The Chamber has ruled that two categories of victims fall within the scope of the Duterte case: (1) victims of murders or attempted murders committed in or around Davao City between 1 November 2011 and 30 June 2016, and (2) victims of murders or attempted murders committed anywhere in the Philippines between 30 June 2016 and 16 March 2019 during his administration’s war on drugs.

Noting the chamber’s decision, the Registry specified that “unless instructed otherwise”, the VPRS will assess applications related to murders and attempted murders that fall outside the scope as “Group B”, or applications that do not clearly qualify as victims.
Those who clearly qualify as victims are categorized in Group A, but the exact number now remains unclear because of the new Registry report.
Meanwhile, applicants for whom the Registry could not make a clear determination for any reason are placed in Group C.
Murders beyond Davao and missing victims
The Registry has also asked Trial Chamber III to decide on several categories of Group C applications.

It seeks guidance on whether the temporal scope includes murders committed in June 2016, as is the case of eight applications that relate to allegations of murders committed in other Philippine locations other than Davao City in the same month.
The Registry also raised the second category of cases involving people who disappeared under circumstances allegedly consistent with drug-war killings.

One applicant reported harm arising from the disappearance of a direct victim, but the VPRS said it remains unclear whether such cases can legally be treated as murder in the absence of proof of death.
In the example cited in the filing, the direct victim has been missing for “more than 10 years.”
The Registry asked judges whether it may rely on a presumption of death in assessing such applications and, if so, what period of disappearance should be sufficient.
“Indirect victims” who witnessed part of crimes

Another clarification the Registry seeks concerns the “distinct category” of indirect victims, those who witnessed “part of the conduct” of crimes, or those with a “pre-existing relationship” to the victim other than a family bond.

One application that the VPRS received was submitted by “a neighbor” who “personally observed the alleged perpetrators proceeding towards the victim’s house” and had heard “several consecutive gunshots”.
The incident caused the applicant’s suffering of “immense fear and trauma [...] from any loud noises and bangs,” the Registry noted.

“In particular, the VPRS notes that the applicant did not witness the killing itself but observed events leading up to it and heard the gunshots. These events may constitute a continuous and closely connected sequence, in time and place, through which the applicant directly perceived the crime as it unfolded.”
Children born after the crimes
Another application was submitted on behalf of a child born three years and six months after the alleged crime in which a relative was killed.
The Registry said the application described the impact on the child of the “psychological and material harm suffered by the family in relation to the murder.”
It asked whether children born into families that continue to experience “significant and ongoing negative consequences” from an alleged crime should themselves be recognized as indirect victims.
More applications expected
The Registry said it received 46 complete applications, comprising 96 individuals, filed as Group A and four others classified as Group C in the latest batch.

It also acknowledged that the number of applications received so far “remains low compared with both the number of WoD [war on drugs] victims and the projected number of victim applications set out in the VPRS Update and Forecast.”
Among the factors cited were VPRS’ difficulties directly assisting victims with applications and limited human and financial resources “in light of multiple competing assignments/situations.”

More applications may still reach the court. The Registry said it is “provisionally planning” another Group A transmission before the trial begins and could continue forwarding applications during the case.
The ICC’s trial of Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Police watchdog to investigate Met’s handling of Meghan warning letter
articles.summary:
IOPC launches independent investigation after referral by Scotland Yard over 2019 letter about Thomas Markle

Scotland Yard faces an independent investigation into its failure in 2019 to pass…
articles.byline: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

blocks.text: Scotland Yard faces an independent investigation into its failure in 2019 to pass claims alleging wrongdoing by Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex, to law enforcement agencies overseas.

The force had referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct over its handling of a letter written by Markle’s former wife, Roslyn Loveless. Markle, 82, is now facing claims of child sexual abuse in the Philippines, which he denies, and is under investigation by authorities there.
On Friday, the IOPC decided to use its formal powers to launch an investigation into the Met. The police watchdog views the claims in the 2019 letter as potentially alleging serious offending.

Its investigation will look at who in the Met made decisions such as not to pass on the claims to police forces in countries where wrongdoing by Markle was alleged, and whether police policies and procedures were followed.

An IOPC spokesperson said: “Following a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, we have decided an independent investigation is required into its failure to pass on allegations of serious offending, contained in a letter it received in 2019, to relevant overseas authorities at the time.”

The Met had announced on Thursday its voluntary referral to the IOPC about the handling of the 2019 letter. It also referred whether its decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duchess of Sussex could have been a breach of data rules because it contained sensitive information. The IOPC has decided it will not investigate that.

The contents of the letter are understood to have played a part in Meghan’s estrangement from her father. The Guardian understands that the long letter made claims about Markle’s activities in the US, the Philippines and Thailand.

The Met has said it did not investigate because the allegations related to potential unlawful activity overseas. But for seven years it did not pass on details to the countries affected, and it is only now sending details of the letter to the FBI in the US and law enforcement in the Philippines, where Markle lived until May, as well as Thai counterparts.

Markle, now in the US, has admitted paying for sex but denies possessing material that would be illegal. On Saturday the Philippine interior minister, Jonvic Remulla, told the Guardian that all signs pointed to Markle being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” and that a full forensic investigation would give a “definitive picture”.
Investigators in the Philippines are examining digital images alleged to belong to Markle and alleged to have been found at his former home in the south-east Asian country.

Meghan’s half-brother, also called Thomas, reported to Philippine authorities last week the alleged discovery of child sexual abuse images. Footage on Thursday showed Markle Jr present as Philippine officials started gathering material to examine.
The scale of embarrassment for the Met will depend on whether investigators in the Philippines assess that the allegations relating to child sexual abuse images have any credence.

On Thursday the Met commander Adam Slonecki, who leads its protection command, said the letter had been sent in 2019 to the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre. “The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom,” he said.

“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”

articles.title: 5 unforgettable Patrick Stewart performances as Jean-Luc Picard
articles.summary: Patrick Stewart had dozens of credits on the screen and the stage, but for many people he will always be Capt. Jean-Luc Picard of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701-D. Here are five of Stewart's best…

image.caption: Patrick Stewart attends the Los Angeles premiere of the third and final season of Paramount+'s original series Star Trek: Picard at TCL Chinese Theatre on Feb. 9, 2023, in Hollywood, Calif. (David Livingston/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Patrick Stewart had dozens of credits on the screen and the stage, but for many people he will always be Capt. Jean-Luc Picard of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701-D. Here are five of Stewart's best Picard performances to seek out.
Stewart brought emotional ferocity and humanist integrity to bear in his portrayal of the Enterprise captain

Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at the age of 86, had dozens of credits to his name on screen and stage over a more than 60-year career, but for many people he will always be Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701-D.
Many Reddit threads and YouTube comments marking Stewart's death are mourning Picard as much as the real man.
"RIP Captain," one Reddit user posted. "You helped change my life for the better."
"Picard was an incredibly well-written and well-acted character that Stewart made real," replied another.

Though Picard had his moments in four movies and on the recent sequel show Star Trek: Picard, the very best moments of the character are all within the 176 episodes of Star Trek: The Next Generation, which ran from 1987 to 1994.
Tributes pour in for X-Men, Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart
Here are five of Stewart's best Picard performances to seek out. (Warning: Spoilers in the descriptions.)
'Make now always the most precious time'
'The Inner Light,' Season 5, Episode 25
Often argued for as the best Star Trek episode of the almost 1,000 made so far, "The Inner Light" is a Stewart tour de force.

When an alien probe knocks the captain unconscious, he wakes up as a villager on a dying planet. In what passes for 25 minutes on the Enterprise, the childless Picard lives for four decades as a man named Kamin, aging before our eyes and raising two children to adulthood.

items: Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
Hugh Jackman, William Shatner, Seth MacFarlane among stars honouring the late Patrick Stewart

blocks.text: The entire episode is a masterpiece, but Stewart imbues simple moments of family with a ferocity and humanist integrity that has made many Trek fans weep.
"Seize the time, Meribor. Live now," he tells his adult daughter as they contemplate the imminent end of their planet. "Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again."
'There are four lights!'
'Chain of Command,' Part II, Season 6, Episode 11
Stewart prepared for this episode, where Picard is brutally tortured, by reviewing tapes provided by Amnesty International, a group Stewart supported and spoke for.

Much of the episode is him alone in a room with another esteemed British actor, the late David Warner. Their scenes crackle with intensity as Cardassian officer (read: space Nazi) Gul Madred attempts to brainwash the captain into thinking there are five lights shining in the room, when there are in fact only four.

The episode offers a brutal depiction of suffering that Stewart throws his full body into. It also contains maybe the biggest "Hell yeah!" moment in the series when Picard refuses to break, yelling, "There are four lights!"

But even better is Stewart's haunted face in the final scene, when he admits the torture had worked, that he would have told his captor anything, and that "more than that, I believed that I could see five lights."
Star Trek, X-Men actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
'Shaka, when the walls fell'
'Darmok,' Season 5, Episode 2
Picard is captured on a planet by an alien race that cannot communicate clearly with humans.

Over the course of the episode, Picard and his crew come to realize that the Children of Tama speak entirely in metaphor, using phrases like "Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra" to mean "co-operation" and "Shaka, when the walls fell" to mean "failure."

Stewart shines twice: first, in a campfire scene, where he tells his alien counterpart the story of the Epic of Gilgamesh; second, when he saves the day by communicating with the Children of Tama's ship, speaking an invented language in a way that is nevertheless commanding and affecting.
Stewart signs a Star Trek: Deep Space Nine banner in Las Vegas on Aug. 14, 2005. Stewart played Picard in that spinoff's pilot. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)
'There is nothing left but dry bones ... dead friends'
'Sarek,' Season 3, Episode 23
This episode features Mark Lenard as the Vulcan Sarek, the father of Mr. Spock from the original 1966 Star Trek series.

Sarek is dying of the sci-fi equivalent of Alzheimer's disease and Picard joins minds with him so that the Vulcan can carry out one last mission. The mind-meld makes Sarek more stable, but floods Picard with a lifetime of repressed emotion.
In an almost four-minute scene, Stewart screams, rants, smiles, cries, fights, longs, regrets, embodies Sarek as portrayed by Lenard — and finally, crumples. It's impossible to look away.
Stewart in 1998's Star Trek: Insurrection. (Getty Images)
'I would rather die as the man I was...'
'Tapestry,' Season 6, Episode 15
In Star Trek's take on It's a Wonderful Life, a dead Picard is visited in the afterlife by recurring guest antagonist Q, who offers him the chance to do his life over.
Stewart gets to play Picard as his usual self, as a brash, young ensign, and as an uncertain, middle-management version of himself that happens in Q's alternate reality.

Stewart caps it off by getting stabbed through the heart (as needs to happen in the "right" reality), looking at the blade and laughing. A scene that could have been hokey is not just believable, but exhilarating.
Episodes of Star Trek: The Next Generation are available to stream on Paramount+ in Canada.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV becomes first pontiff to vote in a US election
articles.summary: The Chicago-born pontiff, who has a tense relationship with Trump, mailed in a ballot for the midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV has submitted his mail-in ballot in Illinois, for the midterm elections, becoming the first-ever pope to vote in a US election.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Holy See Press Office said in a statement.
The Chicago-born pontiff is the first US citizen to hold the Vatican's highest seat, after his selection in May 2025.
Since then, he has clashed with the Trump administration over various issues, including immigration enforcement and the US-Israel war with Iran.
"Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the press office said, including during his years in Peru.
The US midterm elections will determine which political party controls Congress and have a significant impact on the final years of Donald Trump's presidency.
Elections will be held nationwide on 3 November, but early voting has begun in most states.
According to NBC News, the Pope requested his mail-in ballot from the Will County Clerk's Office on 3 October.
Less than two weeks later, the Vatican announced he had surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung after he was diagnosed with lung cancer.
The Vatican confirmed last week that the Pope, aged 71, will travel as planned to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru in early November.
Tensions escalated between the Pope and the US president in April, after the Pope called for peace in the wake of US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
"I don't think he's doing a very good job," Trump said about the Pope afterwards.
"We don't like a Pope that's going to say that it's OK to have a nuclear weapon," he continued. "I'm not a big fan of Pope Leo."
Pope Leo followed with his own remarks later, saying: "The mission of the Church is to preach the Gospel, to preach peace," according to Reuters.
"If someone wants to criticise me for preaching the Gospel... I hope simply to be listened to because of the value of God's words."
In the final few days before the midterms, Republican and Democratic officials alike are sprinting across the country to boost their party's chances of success.

Polls suggest Democrats are the favourite to gain control of the lower chamber of Congress, called the House of Representatives, and are poised to win seats in Republican-leaning areas that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election.
Democrats also appear to have a chance to win additional seats in the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress.
The gloomy outlook for Trump's Republican party has seen the president hold several rallies in states where Republican victories are typically all but guaranteed.

articles.title: Germany news: Merz hopes for Korean reunification at DMZ
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expressed hope for Korean reunification during a visit to the heavily fortified border. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier has held talks with China's Xi Jinping in…
articles.byline: Richard Connor, Matt Ford, Wesley Rahn, Alex Berry

image.caption: South Korea is the final stop on Merz's five-day Asia tour, following visits to Singapore and JapanImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026last updated October 30, 2026
Merz at DMZ says he hopes Korea can reunify like Germany did

blocks.caption: Merz visited the "T2" barrack building at the DMZImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.
North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.

blocks.caption: Merz briefly stepped into the 'North Korean side' behind a conference table in the border barrack buildingImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.
"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he said.

"You can also notice it here at this place, how much a country suffers from division and how strong the desire is for reunification, at least in this part of the Korean Peninsula," he said, adding that he had been asked about Germany's reunification experience while visiting Seoul.

North Korea, however, has backed away in recent years from diplomacy with the South, having officially removed language calling for reunification from its constitution while changing the South's status to that of a "hostile state."

articles.title: Cost of living protests to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Halloween
articles.summary: Activists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housing
articles.byline: Deborah Cole in Berlin and Jon Henley in Paris

blocks.text: Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies.

Weeks of, at times violent, student demonstrations have rocked Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania and France, where activists on Halloween have again called for people to make their anger over the cost of living and deficient public services felt across the country.

In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service.

blocks.caption: Students and activists block access to the Andreas-Gymnasium in Berlin this month in protest against compulsory military service and education cuts. Photograph: snapshot-photography/F Boillot/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.”
But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.

“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.
Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.
“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.

About 10,000 protesters, mainly pupils, students and their parents, are expected at the Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, with another smaller gathering planned in the early evening in the Mitte district.
Large rallies have also been called in Cologne, Munich, Frankfurt and Hamburg.

The team behind Gen Z regelt has used social media and its website to call on participants to exercise restraint: “Our protest is peaceful, without exception. Violence goes against everything we stand for. Only through peaceful means can we achieve something together.”
By Friday, more than 160,000 people had registered on the website saying they planned to attend the protests.

The federal pupils’ conference, a youth political lobbying group, has distanced itself from Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the initiative’s “unclear” organisational structure made the events unpredictable.
It plans to hold a separate protest in Berlin on 20 November that will include teachers and other youth movements focused on the marked decline in German school performance.

In France, the interior minister, Laurent ⁠Nuñez, said Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day, adding that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the sidelines of the new wave of protests.
after newsletter promotion

Nuñez said late on Thursday that radical groups had called on social media for violent Halloween gatherings and that the biggest threat to public order would probably come after mainstream cost-of-living demonstrations had officially ended.

“We are seeing many calls from the labour movement, the radicalised far left and certain radicalised gilets jaunes [yellow vests], urging people to attend rallies on public streets starting at 8pm in many cities ‌across France,” he said.

The calls were “accompanied by various messages which are quite radical”, Nuñez added, including some demanding “revolution”. He said authorities would “tolerate zero excesses” and promised an “extremely firm” security response.

blocks.caption: Protesters holding a French flag amid clashes during demonstrations in Paris last Saturday. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters

blocks.text: Measures introduced last weekend to protect shops would be reinforced, Nuñez said, and while peaceful demonstrations would be authorised, most would not be permitted “in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.

It is unclear what will happen in Paris. Two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. Both sets of organisers are challenging the decision to exclude them from the centre.

The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October.

Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide ​strike called for 5 November.

Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.

articles.title: Christa Pike says she's in 'constant pain' since surviving execution attempt
articles.summary: Convicted murderer Christa Pike says while she continues to get stronger, she has been in pain since surviving a botched execution in Tennessee last month.

image.caption: This photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike on Jan. 12, 2023. Pike says while she continues to get stronger, she has been in pain since surviving a botched execution in Tennessee last month. (Tennessee Department of Correction via The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Convicted murderer Christa Pike says while she continues to get stronger, she has been in pain since surviving a botched execution in Tennessee last month.
Pike survived 2 doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts," said Pike in a statement that was dictated to her legal team and released Friday.
"I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."

Pike survived two doses of the drug pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death in the U.S.

items: Tennessee may try to execute Christa Pike again. The state could face legal hurdles

blocks.text: The slaying involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and taking a chunk of her skull as a souvenir.
The execution attempt initially left Pike unconscious and on a ventilator, with severe arm injuries. She was hospitalized but has since returned to the prison where she was serving her sentence.
Pike is the first person known to have survived being injected with a full lethal dose of execution drugs.
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger. But healing is not the same as being OK," she said.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," Pike said.
In her statement, Pike said she had walked into the execution chamber "prepared to die" and had "made my peace."
"I had also told the people in the room and who were there to witness my execution that I was leaving them in loving kindness."
Instead, she said, she woke up several days later "alone in a hospital confused and in pain."
"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position."
Pike said she has received "extraordinary love and support" from people around the world.

"To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words. It is humbling, and it has touched me more deeply than I can explain."
'Don't know why I survived'
Pike also thanked the first responders, doctors, nurses and hospital staff who cared for her.
"I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time."

Pike's attorneys have urged Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to reduce Pike's sentence to life imprisonment. Lee told reporters earlier this week that, "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts."
Following the unsuccessful execution attempt, Lee halted further executions for the remainder of the year and ordered a comprehensive third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.
Meanwhile, a Tennessee judge has ordered that all evidence from the attempted execution be preserved so a full investigation can take place.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Mark Gollom is a Toronto-based reporter with CBC News. He covers Canadian and U.S. politics and current affairs.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Over 436K passengers pass through NAIA ahead of Undas weekend
articles.summary: More than 436,000 passengers have passed through the Ninoy Aquino International Airport from Oct. 27 to Oct. 29 ahead of the long weekend for Undas, or the Philippines' observance of All Saints' Day…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 10:11pm

More than 436,000 passengers have passed through the Ninoy Aquino International Airport from Oct. 27 to Oct. 29 ahead of the long weekend for Undas, or the Philippines' observance of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day on Sunday and Monday.
According to JP Soriano's report on Friday, the Philippine National Police (PNP) are on full alert at the airport as hundreds of thousands of people travel during the season.
One of them was John Lawrence Soliva, a maritime school student in Manila who was headed back to Palawan for the solemn holiday. He carried with him boxes of donuts for his family at home.
“Family gathering po, nagdadala po kami ng mga pagkain po, doon po kami nagsasalo-salo nanananghalian, kwentuhan lang, bonding lang po as family,” Soliva said.
(It is a family gathering; we bring food, and we get together there to eat, talk, just bonding as a family.)

While some are going home to celebrate Undas, others are leaving the country. Overseas Filipino Worker (OFW) Mary Jane Martinez is headed back to Milan, Italy after having an early Undas commemoration.
“Yung lolo po namin kasi ay namatay siya na wala ako, kaya promise ko na pagdating ko, titingnan ko siya at pag-alis ko, dapat makapagpaalam din ako sa kanya,” Martinez said.
(Our grandfather died while I was not here, so I promised that when I come back, I will look at him and then when I leave, I will also bid farewell to him.)

Airport authorities are also still monitoring whether the explosion of Mayon Volcano will affect flights, but as of this evening, no Albay flights have been affected. Residents may check their emails and follow the news to see if their flights have been canceled. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockery
articles.summary:
Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms

Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.

Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the United States after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – declare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.

“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaper thundered on Friday.

Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.

But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.

Perhaps most bizarrely, the far-right absconder claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.

“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.

Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.

The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.
Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted a ferocious outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.
“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator, told the network GloboNews.

The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.

blocks.caption: A woman reads a newspaper with news of the election result on Monday in São Paulo. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.
José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”
Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.

Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,” Malafaia was quoted as saying by O Globo.

Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying rightwing”.

The Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.
Others warn Bolsonarismo will remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement is now in doubt.

Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, Homeland and Family”, which became “Goodbye, Homeland and Family”.

Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São Paulo called Lula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.
Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, Trump replied: “I won’t get involved.”

articles.title: Seoul fears being sidelined as US reaches out to North Korea
articles.summary: With ties between South Korea and the Trump administration strained, the South Korean government worries that Donald Trump's pursuit of a diplomatic breakthrough with Kim Jong Un may come at Seoul's…

image.caption: South Korea has been facing pressure both from North Korea and from its ally, the United StatesImage: Evan Vucci/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Korea's relationship with the North, always strained, seems to be going through a particularly hostile patch in recent weeks.

Last month, Seoul accused North Korea of planting a mine on the southern side of the heavily fortified border. The device exploded, injuring three South Korean soldiers. Pyongyang refused to apologize and insisted this was a false-flag incident designed to tarnish the isolated nation. The North Korean regime has since conducted multiple weapons tests, held its first-ever exhibition of military drones attended by Kim Jong Un, brought up self-propelled artillery units to the border and started preparing loudspeaker systems that will blast propaganda into the South.
On Thursday, North Korea also fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the Sea of Japan just before a scheduled visit to South Korea by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

On top of South Korea's issues with its arch rival, many in Seoul are growing increasingly wary of their most important ally, the United States. South Korean politicians are worried that the US could push for a diplomatic breakthrough with North Korea at the cost of ignoring South Korea's security, or even leave it exposed to Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal.
Who gets a voice on South Korea's future?

US President Donald Trump famously claimed he and Kim Jong Un "fell in love" during Trump's first term. More recently, Trump has indicated he would like to resume talks . There have been suggestions that a meeting could take place on November 18 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Why North Korea is now Europe's problem

The North Korean side has made no official response to Washington's hints, although South Korea's National Intelligence Service informed a closed-door meeting of Seoul's intelligence committee on Thursday that Kim Jong Un discussed the possibility of meeting Trump when he met with senior members of China's politburo in Dandong on Saturday.

Seoul's fears were also fueled by the US proposing three-way talks with Russia and China on the fate of Ukraine without inviting a representative of Kyiv to attend. The worry in Seoul is that President Donald Trump may conduct a similar bypass manoeuvre on the Korean Peninsula.
Washington-Seoul relationship shaken by tariffs, funding disputes

"Right now, there is a problem of trust between the two governments," said Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation.

A security and trade relationship that was previously considered secure has been rocked by tariffs, trade restrictions and demands from Washington that the South pay more for the US troops stationed in the country, Kim told DW.
President Lee's diplomats have lost access to key decision-making personnel in this White House, he added.

"I do not think this US administration is thinking long-term in the relationship with South Korea," Kim said. "They do not see South Korea as a part of their wider national security network and I do not think they are listening to experts on the importance of allies in the region."
"I also think that Trump is eager to meet with Kim because of his personal quest to obtain a Nobel Peace Prize."

Trump's widely publicized efforts to secure a Nobel have been thwarted so far. However, this might change if Trump somehow manages to formally end the Korean War that was put on hold by the 1953 armistice.
South Korea eyeing its own nuclear deterrent

"The most serious concern is that the US recognizes Pyongyang as a nuclear power, which would legitimize the North's program and undermine efforts to convince it to abolish its nuclear weapons as well as the broader non-proliferation system," said Lim Eun-jung, a professor of international studies at Kongju National University.

In parallel, she said, there are fears that Trump could reach an agreement with North Korea that requires it to scrap its long-range nuclear missiles — those that are capable of hitting targets in the United States — but permits it to retain short-range weapons that can still easily reach South Korea and Japan.

That would raise questions about the US commitment to defend South Korea in case of a nuclear attack. That uncertainty, in turn, is likely to give credence to voices arguing that South Korea needs to develop its own nuclear deterrent.

"For years, we have depended on US extended deterrence guarantees under the nuclear umbrella, but this US administration is unpredictable and there are more and more people asking why we don't just go it alone," Lim told DW.
"Virtually, all our neighbors have nuclear weapons, and while no-one wants the dominoes to start falling, it could happen."
Merz says Korean security affects Europe

The latest escalation between Seoul and Pyongyang comes amid repeated attempts by South Korean President Lee to improve communication with Pyongyang. The perceived outreach has irritated South Korea's European allies, who are angry over North Korea deploying soldiers and supplying munition and missiles to help Russia in the Ukraine war.
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs
Moscow is believed to be repaying Pyongyang's support with money, military technology and security guarantees.
During his visit to South Korea, Germany's Merz pointed out that "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects the security of Korea."
"The world is small — even in war," Merz added.
South Korea needs allies

Berlin, just like Seoul, has been disoriented by the Trump administration turning hostile on many of its allies while seeking reproachment with geopolitical rivals such as Russia and China. During his Asia tour, Merz pushed for an alliance of middle powers to protect free trade and oppose "unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law."

blocks.caption: German Chancellor Merz recently visited South Korea along with Japan and SingaporeImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The fact remains that the United States is shifting its foreign policy, ⁠its foreign economic ​policy, and redefining its interests. As they do so, we must do the same," he said in South Korea.

It was not clear if Seoul will respond to Merz's appeal by moving closer to the European Union. At the moment, however, it seems apparent that the South Korean government is struggling to communicate with either North Korea or the US.
"It is a very difficult situation," said Kim Sang-woo. "There is no trust and no connections and that, to me, is very worrisome."

articles.title: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case
articles.summary:
Scraping copyrighted material from internet could ‘potentially’ amount to acquisition of property by government, Anne Twomey says

  • Get our

blocks.text: Altering copyright law to allow AI companies to scrape music, books and journalism could trigger a constitutional breach, Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned, as they raise new fears it could open Australia to massive legal action and compensation claims from rights holders worldwide.

The attorney general’s department admitted it was “extremely alive” to the issue, and Australia’s leading constitutional expert, Anne Twomey, agreed there was “potentially” a concern – depending how legislation was drafted – that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.

In a simmering debate centred on the same legal point as the movie The Castle, the question of acquiring property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern amid furious lobbying from tech companies and rights holders ahead of a looming federal government announcement on AI.
“We could be liable for ‘just terms’ compensation for acquiring that property for every rights holder on Earth,” Ross Cadell, a Nationals senator, told Guardian Australia.
Michaelia Cash, the shadow attorney general, said the government should not “sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment”.

Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of reforms around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.

Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder deployed digital protections signaling an objection.

A fresh concern being aired by sceptics and creatives is that any weakening of copyright to benefit AI could represent a breach of section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about “the acquisition of property on just terms”.

“If they go ahead with an opt-out model, it does raise a real question of whether the government is acquiring the intellectual property rights of others,” said Cadell, a member of the federal parliamentary committee on AI.
“How we support property rights is core to this.”

A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.

Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said the issue was exceedingly complex and noted no legislative proposal had been aired. She said numerous cases had come before the high court relating to copyright and acquisition of property, including about video games, cigarette plain packaging and cassette tapes, with varying outcomes.

Twomey expected the federal government would be hyperaware of such concerns, but said granting a new right to AI companies to use copyrighted material and diminishing the rights of copyright holders could “potentially” trigger constitutional issues.

“The high court has recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 … One would want to be quite confident before enacting the legislation about whether or not section 51 would apply,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.
She said any change allowing Australia to host AI companies training on international data could potentially create grounds for global rights holders to take legal action here.
Cadell told Guardian Australia he worried about such a development opening the federal government to liability for “the biggest compensation rights case in history”.
after newsletter promotion
Cadell raised his concerns about the constitution in a committee hearing with the attorney general’s department on Friday, in which officials said they were conscious of those issues.
Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders.
Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow AI companies to scrape data was “clearly an acquisition of property”.

“It’s hard to imagine what kind of compensation would make up for the fact that they’re basically taking our right … and trading it away to the AI companies to then monetise themselves, and that appears to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge.”

Chris Maund, CEO of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals.
He also raised concern about international ramifications were Australia to change copyright law, saying it would not only apply to Australian artists and copyright owners.

“The AI company could do their training here in Australia and circumvent the copyright laws that apply outside of Australia, and that’s why the international creative industries are watching this very closely,” he said.

Maund said international rights holder groups had been urging Labor not to weaken copyright law. Guardian Australia has provided submissions to the Joint Select Committee as a member of Australia’s wider rights holder community.

“The Australian government has been really great to the music industry, particularly Prime Minister Albanese and Tony Burke. They’ve set up Creative Music Australia, which companies like us and our artists have done very well out of, but it feels like they’re out of step with artists and copyright owners on this point,” he said.
Cash said the Coalition welcomed the benefits of AI and wanted investment, but also raised the constitutional concern.
“That is the prime minister’s own test, and the government should be held to it,” she said of compensation to rights holders.
“The constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms is also a live issue we will be examining depending on what the government puts forward.”
Cadell said while AI had benefits, he worried about its risks.
“There’s lots of talk about what the benefits may be and what may happen. But if we take these rights away, we know what will happen,” Cadell said.
“I don’t want to hurt people for a ‘may’.”

articles.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
articles.summary: A wave of shootings and extortion threats has rattled India's film industry. This time, those claiming responsibility are very different from the Mumbai underworld that had Bollywood in its grip back…

image.caption: Indian actor Tiger Shroff (center) was recently shot at in Mumbai [FILE March 17, 2017]Image: Amal KS/Hindustan Times/IMAGO

blocks.text: "In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed."
This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting.

The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang's involvement.
The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as "Bollywood".

Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan's apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani's family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million (around €980,000).
The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe, with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times.

For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago.
When the underworld ruled Bollywood
In the 1990s, Mumbai's underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry.

"The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry," said S. Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of "Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia," who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades.
Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel "were totally obsessed" with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood.

blocks.caption: During his era, Dawood Ibrahim has been one of the most wanted men in IndiaImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films "so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money," Zaidi added.

When producers didn't cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded.
Mumbai's streets were "made red with blood" in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings.
D. Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one "every third day," mostly over unpaid extortion demands.

Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the "ultimate weapon." Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons.
"A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts.
By the early 2000s, the gangs' hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging.
A gang run from a prison cell
The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai.

blocks.caption: Lawrence Bishnoi was a student politician in the northern city of Chandigarh before gaining notoriety as a gangsterImage: Sameer Sehgal/Hindustan Times/IMAGO

blocks.text: Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of "Gangs of Punjab."
"He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail," Singh told DW.

Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps.
Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat.

His network stretches beyond India's borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi's group in North America.
While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online.

"There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi," Singh explained. "Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons."
Why target film stars?
For Bishnoi, it seems personal.

In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi's community. Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang.
Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals "always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian," he says, and this case was Bishnoi's "chance to redeem himself."

blocks.caption: Salman Khan was granted bail in 2018 as he appealed a conviction for killing two rare antelopesImage: AFP

blocks.text: But money and intimidation matter too.
"Bollywood has a lot of money," Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage.
"With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that."

Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole "basket" of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were "local boys," while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is "loaded with money" and a "soft underbelly."
"They are using Bollywood as an ATM," he told DW. "Insert a card and collect your money."

Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. "It's a way to grab headlines," he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called "absolutely illogical and absurd."

But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. "The base material of extortion is: create fear," a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW.
Is Bollywood under siege?
Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave.

"I won't say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration," Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi's faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai.
The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added.
India's banned film 'Satluj' finds new audiences

Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are "all aimed at collecting… extortion money," he said. In his view, "cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people."
At any case, the fear remains real.
And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods.

"If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai," the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah.
"Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear," Gupta wrote.
With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign.
Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security.

articles.title: Fewer households biking in 2026 --SWS
articles.summary: The Social Weather Stations (SWS) found that the number of households that used bicycles has declined to 26% in 2026.

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 9:53pm
The Social Weather Stations (SWS) found that the number of households that used bicycles has declined to 26% in 2026.
This is a 10% decline from the cycling peak in 2023, which was 36% of households nationwide.
In a survey taken from June 20 to 29, only 26% or 7.3 million households were “cycling households,” or those who have at least one member who cycled for any activity.
The previous years recorded the cycling households as follows:

items: 2021: 24% (6.2 million households)
2022: 29% (7.3 million households)
2023: 36% (10 million households)
2024: 28% (7.7 million households)

blocks.text: Most cyclists do so for recreational purposes rather than essential activities, according to the SWS. However, there has been a reduction in both types of cyclists.

When asked why they cycled, 35% of respondents said that it was to improve health, while 32% said that it was for work or transportation. Other reasons cited included recreation, to save money, to socialize, and more.
For households that did not cycle, most of them (58%) cited not having a bike as a reason.
As of June 2026, there were 23% of Filipino households that owned a bicycle, which led to a ratio of bicycle owners to car owners being 5:1.

“Twenty-six national SWS surveys from May 2020 to June 2026 show that there were more bicycle owners compared to car owners nationwide. In all twenty-six surveys, the bulk of motor vehicle owners nationwide own 2-wheeled types, such as motorcycles,” the SWS said.
The SWS said that 46% of households nationwide owned a 2-wheeled motor vehicle, 17% owned a 3-wheeled motor vehicle, and 5% owned 4-wheeled motor vehicles.

According to the SWS, electronically-assisted bicycles comprised a small portion of bicycle-owning households, with only 681,000 owning them. While this number is a small part of the sample, the polling firm has noted an increase in electronically assisted bikes since 2024.

For motor vehicles, electric models are also the minority, with an estimated 871,000 households owning electric 2-wheeled motor vehicles. Gas-powered models still account for the majority of two-wheel, three-wheel, and four-wheel vehicles.

The survey interviewed 1,200 adults, with 300 each from Metro Manila, Balance Luzon (Luzon areas outside of Metro Manila), Visayas, and Mindanao. The survey has a sampling error of ±3% for national percentages. —LDF, GMA News
