2023: 128 cadavers
2024: 135 cadavers
2025: 151 cadavers

blocks.text: Correctional Technical / Corrections Chief Superintendent (CT/CSUPT) Ma. Cecilia Villanueva, BuCor Deputy Director General for Reformation, explained that families are unable to claim the deceased persons deprived of liberty (PDL) because their homes are far.
"Usually yung mga tawid-dagat, yung malalayo, Visayas, Mindanao, but we send letters," Villanueva told GMA News Online.
(Those people cross the seas; they are from Visayas and Mindanao, but we send letters.)
Once a PDL is declared dead, the body is brought to Eastern Funeral Home in Muntinlupa City for documentation, while the Bureau of Corrections contacts the deceased’s family.
However, in some cases, family members cannot be contacted, or no one claims the bodies due to financial constraints, while others just retrieve the death certificates.
Unclaimed bodies are then buried in the New Bilibid Prison Cemetery, also in Muntinlupa City.
“Kasi kahit sabihin naman natin na mga PDL, they have the same rights as any public person,” Villanueva said.
“Meron din silang dignidad kahit pa naman sabihin natin na mga PDL ’yan. May dignity pa rin in their death," she added.
(Even though they are PDLs, they have the same rights as any public person. They still have dignity, even in death.)
BuCor data showed the highest number of unclaimed bodies in 2021 (285 cadavers) and 2020 (258 cadavers), the years when the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted operations worldwide.
“Yung period namin for [claiming the deceased persons] lumampas nga sa 60 days. Kasi nga, may mga limitations sa movement,” Villanueva said.
(Our period for claiming the deceased exceeded 60 days due to restrictions on movement.)
“Kahit nga yung cremated, yung iba hindi na nila claim yung remains ng relatives nila,” Villanueva said, adding that PDLs who died from the coronavirus were immediately cremated.
(Even those that were cremated, some relatives were unable to claim them.)
According to the BuCor data, 89 cremated bodies were claimed while 23 were unclaimed.
Left behind

Quezon City’s Burial Assistance Program serves indigent residents by providing free burial services. Vivs Funeral Homes is one of the funeral parlors accredited by the local government in the project.
Vivs Funeral Homes Operations Manager Larry Leccio said that although rare, there have been instances when they had to bury an unclaimed body.
There are various reasons why bodies go unclaimed, Leccio explained. In some cases, they belong to impoverished people who die on the streets and are brought to hospitals.
“Itong isang patay ay dinala ng pamilya niya sa ospital doon sa East Avenue. Tapos, hindi na binalikan. Tapos hindi na mahanap yung pamilya,” Leccio said.
(One of the dead was brought by the family to the hospital there in East Avenue. After that, they did not come back. And the family could no longer be found.)

The process typically began at the hospital, according to Leccio. The hospital then alerts the barangay, which makes a report. Details about the found body are then circulated in newspapers for 30 days in hopes of finding a claimant. During those 30 days, the body remains at the morgue of the funeral home.
However, once the body hits the 60-day mark, the local government needs to act on the matter.

Since the Quezon City local government has a free funeral service program, a barangay representative will be interviewed by the city’s Social Services Development Department on behalf of the unclaimed body.
Once local government officials handle all the necessary documentation, the funeral parlor can process the death certificate.

In case that no one knows the body’s name, the cadavers are simply issued a case number and labeled as “unknown” before being buried in a public cemetery. Their tombstones would also be labeled as such, Leccio said.
There would be no ceremonies for the body.
“Direct na libing na po siya. Wala na po siyang pamisa,” Leccio said. (It is a direct burial. There will be no masses.)
The dead as a teacher

Despite the initial shock of seeing the cadavers before them, Sta. Ana said that the students would eventually get used to them because of how invaluable they were as learning instruments — they could even freely go in and out of the laboratory where the cadavers were just to study them.
As the semester went on, the students got used to dealing with the cadavers. So much so that they almost forget that bodies used to be people.

“We still have to remember to be respectful to it, kasi nga, habang na nasasanay ka sa nakikita mo sa harapan mo, nakakalimutan mo na this was a person, this is a person we're dealing with, kahit hindi na siya nagsasalita,” Sta. Ana said.

(We still have to remember to be respectful to it, because while you get used to seeing it in front of you, you forget that this was a person, this is a person we’re dealing with, even if they no longer speak.)
As a result, the students would always begin their sessions with the bodies with a prayer, offering them gratitude.
They had also given the anonymous bodies names, and spoke to them as if they were still alive.
“Mami” was the name of the cadaver assigned to Sta. Ana and her group. She still has a personal bracelet on her wrist, which the students kept on.
Whenever an incision needed to be made, or if skin needed to be pulled back, the students would inform the cadaver that it could hurt and apologize to them.

“We talk to them as if they are still alive, so even if we know that they are physically not with us, we still find a way to talk to them and say ‘thank you’, and say ‘sorry’... it helps us humanize the experience,” Sta. Ana said.

While they knew nothing of the stories of the bodies before them, sometimes, the bodies themselves offered signs of how they died. Both the teachers and students could make their own inferences on how the cadavers wound up dead. Sta. Anna recounted that one of the first bodies she saw had red marks around the neck.

Regardless of how the bodies ended up before the students, one thing was certain: they were invaluable teachers. As physical therapy students, they had to become familiar with human anatomy. And these bodies could teach them things that no book ever could, Sta. Ana said.
They would often go around looking at different types of bodies just to learn more, she added.
Sta. Ana hopes of becoming a doctor one day, a path that would likely introduce her to even more cadavers.
“We recognize that we’re learning so much through their bodies and we understand that they make significant contributions to our education as physical therapists,” Sta. Ana said.
While the bodies that reached Sta. Ana and her classmates were anonymous, it was unlikely that they were prisoners.
Villanueva said the agency has not been providing cadavers to be dissected in medical schools after they were flagged by human rights groups.
“I started in 1998. Parang around that time na pinagbawal ng human rights yung paggamit ng body para sa mga medical schools,” Villanueva shared.
(I started in 1998. Around that time, it was around that time, I think, that the use of bodies for medical school purposes was prohibited after being flagged by human rights groups.)
“Marami naman kaming letter requests from medical schools na hindi namin na-approve,” she added.
Currently, BuCor is looking into building more buildings across the country to decongest existing detention facilities and bring PDLs closer to their families.
“More regional prison facilities [kasi] dapat yung nandito, yung taga-NCR, yung malapit. Eh hindi eh. Marami dito na taga-tawid-dagat pa rin,” Villanueva said.
(BuCor is working on regional prison facilities because PDLs from NCR should be detained here, but that’s not the case. Many PDLs here are from far away areas.)
The Holy Body
We are all made according to God’s likeness, according to Father John Paulo Bautista of the Mary Immaculate Parish in Dasmariñas City.

“The Church teaches very clearly that everybody, every Christian, Catholics or not, every human person, whether it is unclaimed or claimed bodies, we bear the image of God,” Bautista said in an interview.

However, this does not mean that priests could simply bless abandoned bodies, as they may not be certain if the corpses were Catholic when they were still alive, Bautista explained. Priests would need the permission of the deceased’s kin to bless the body.

Bautista recounted a time when he saw a motorcycle rider who died in a road crash incident. While he was initially inclined to give the body blessing, he had to stop and think. Would it have been an act of charity? Would he have to wait for the family?
Priests were not strictly prohibited from blessing a body that they were unsure of being Catholic however, Bautista explained. But it was still discouraged.
In cases where the body is used as a learning instrument — as was the case with the physical therapy students — Bautista maintained that it should be done morally.
“It should be done in a right way, legal way, in a moral way, at the same time, with a reverence to the body,” Bautista said.
“The human body is sacred,” he added.
There are a few ways to honor the unclaimed dead, according to Bautista. For Catholics, they could offer a Mass, prayer, or even the act of remembrance.
But what if there was no one left to remember the dead? Bautista said that Catholics could offer a prayer for a soul in purgatory.

“The Church is praying for them, in Masses, they are remembered… If you will pray for them, generally, we could say prayers for the souls in purgatory, and for those who have not attained a peaceful, holy, or blessed death,” Bautista said. —With GMA News Research/Joviland Rita/ LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos to new Bangsamoro MPs: Serve with humility, good governance
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday called on the newly elected members of the Bangsamoro parliament to serve the people with humility and honor those who fought for peace through…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 5:06pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday called on the newly elected members of the Bangsamoro parliament to serve the people with humility and honor those who fought for peace through good governance.
This, as the President attended the inaugural session of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Parliament at the Bangsamoro Government Center in Cotabato City.
Marcos said that the first session of the BARMM parliament is not just a victory for Mindanao, but the entire country.

“For decades, generations wondered if this day would ever come. Today, we welcome the inaugural session of the first elected Bangsamoro Parliament. This formally ends the seven-year transition under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority and marks the beginning of the region’s first regular parliamentary government,” he said.
“Truly, this is a victory for our Bangsamoro brethren. It is a victory for Mindanao. It is a victory for the entire Filipino nation,” he added.

The President also noted that the event serves as a milestone in the peace process between the national government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), “marking the transition from armed struggle to peaceful democratic governance.”
He however, acknowledged that the path leading up to the conduct of the inaugural session was “long and painful,” with families suffering and losing loved ones during years of conflict.
Under the new phase of parliamentary governance, Marcos said leaders must uphold unity, statesmanship, and cooperation to build a more peaceful and progressive BARMM.

“A stable government means enacting laws and delivering programs and services responsive to the needs of the Bangsamoro people. It also means using public resources efficiently and transparently to create economic opportunities and strengthen regional development,” he explained.
“Above all, it means ensuring that the dividends of peace are felt in the daily lives of every Bangsamoro family,” he continued.
Marcos also committed that the national government will continue to expand economic opportunities for Mindanao, and will continue to support the Bangsamoro autonomy and democratic institutions.

“To the people of the Bangsamoro, the national government stands with you. Your success is the success of the country. Hinding-hindi namin kayo pababayaan (we will never abandon you),” the President said.
The BARMM held its first parliamentary elections on September 14, with a final voter turnout of 84.34%, representing 2,018,478 voters out of the region’s 2.393 million registered voters.

The 80 newly elected Parliament members assumed office today, October 30, and are set to elect the region’s chief minister. The first elected officials will serve a five-year term until June 30, 2031.

Under Republic Act No. 11054 or the Bangsamoro Organic Law, the Parliament will elect the Chief Minister by a majority vote of at least 41 of its 80 members. The Chief Minister will lead the regional government and advance its development priorities, subject to parliamentary oversight. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Houthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city says
articles.summary:
Oxygen, food and water supplies running low and massacres taking place, says Nabil Shamsan

The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in…

blocks.text: The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in a briefing designed to urge the international community to do more to lift the month-long siege.

Nabil Shamsan said massacres were taking place in Yemen’s third city, that oxygen and water supplies were running out and that rubbish was piling up in the streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.

The city’s daily minimum water needs are estimated at about 35,000 cubic metres, he said, but no more than 1,000 cubic metres was being allowed to reach it each day and that water shipments were being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city.
With food stocks depleted and the price of wheat soaring, he said “citizens are heading back to the stone age”. Restaurants had closed due to the lack of fuel.

Shamsan said that as many as 1,800 people were in need of dialysis treatment but were unable to access supplies, that 120 health centres had been suspended and schools had closed, affecting hundreds of thousands of children.

He said 64 people had been killed, including civilians, from August to 20 October 2026 and a further 173 injured. More than 6,400 newly displaced families, each averaging seven members, had come to the city to flee the fighting.
“We are not talking about living, just surviving,” he said.

His account contradicted one given by the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi, who said: “The way is open for food, medicine, and humanitarian aid to enter the city and even for Saudi-backed groups to do so. Anyone who wants to verify that there is no siege on the city of Taiz can go to the city and see.”

blocks.caption: Fuel shortages are threatening neonatal intensive care units in Taiz, where 120 health centres have been suspended.  Photograph: Hamza Mustafa/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Shamsan said that Houthis forces had a near-total grip on the roads into the city, adding the group had issued a choice to the more than 800,000 inside the city “either to leave or to die”.

He accused the Houthis of not waging a military battle but a battle to change the identity of Yemen, with captured villages being taken over by new religious leaders with education and religious curricula being changed. “This is not a military war but a war of vengeance,” he said.

People in occupied territories were being required to show loyalty to the Zaydi religion and to sign forms affirming they had joined the Houthis. “They are not starting a war but an revolution in identity,” Shamsan said, adding that scores of children from each village were being forcibly ordered without their parents’ consent to join the frontlines in Saada and elsewhere.

Vowing the people of Taiz would resist until the end, he said statements of solidarity were of no use and that what was needed was access for aid agencies, including the UN, to deliver supplies to the city.

blocks.caption: Rubbish is piling up in the city’s streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible. Photograph: Hamza Mustafa/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Shamsan was reluctant to divulge details of the state of the military campaign, but said shelling of the city was becoming more frequent and that communication between the city and rural areas had broken down. Houthis now controlled the mobile networks and were sending messages to citizens to end their resistance, while eavesdropping on all conversations, he said. Mobile networks were “completely disrupted”, he said, adding that he was speaking only 2-5km from the frontlines.

Most independent agencies agree that life inside the city is rapidly deteriorating. Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taiz show their utter disregard for civilian lives.
“Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taiz, the Houthis have bombed, starved and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.”

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Marcos didn’t vow to stay in Palace till flood mess ends
articles.summary: Article 7 of the 1987 Constitution limits an elected president to a single six-year term with no eligibility for re-election

blocks.text: Claim: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will not leave the Palace until the flood control scandal is resolved.
Why we fact-checked this: Viral Philippines, a Facebook page with 321,000 followers, posted a supposed quote card of Marcos dated October 24.
The quote read, “Hindi ako aalis sa Malacañang hangga’t hindi naaayos ang problema sa flood control.” (I will not leave Malacañang until the flood control problem is resolved.)
The page captioned it, “Forever na ito sa Malacañang.” (He’s here to stay in Malacañang forever)
The post garnered 23,700 reactions, 4,800 comments, and 522 shares as of writing. Commenters also believed the quote and questioned Marcos’ capability to address the flood control scandal.
The facts: No official records or statements confirm that Marcos made this remark. Nor is there any indication that he intends to remain in office beyond his term to resolve the flood control issue.
In addition, Article 7 of the 1987 Constitution limits an elected president to a single six-year term with no eligibility for reelection.

The President has faced scrutiny over the administration’s handling of the issue. In July, he dismissed calls for his resignation over allegations that the government’s response to flood control problems has been too slow.

He did not voice plans to extend his term; he instead said, “I cannot say that we have done enough because we are not done yet. Unfortunately, the more we look, the more we find. And it is already going back beyond my administration, beyond my term.”

In his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA), Marcos announced that P800 million worth of assets out of P20 billion for flood control funds have been recovered since flagging them in his previous SONA.
In September, Marcos said that a decades-old flood control master plan for Luzon is finally being implemented.
Flood control arrests: After the 2025 SONA, multiple investigations have resulted in the arrests of high-profile individuals linked to flood control corruption.

These include contractor Sarah Discaya, Senator Jinggoy Estrada, former Department of Public Works and Highways secretary Manuel Bonoan (released after being announced as turning into a state witness), and Congressman and Marcos’ cousin Martin Romualdez.

Meanwhile, former Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co has been on the run and out of the country since 2025. He’s facing another graft and malversation case filed by the Office of the Ombudsman in August, besides a similar case filed before the Sandiganbayan in November 2025.

Extending or stepping down: Rappler has debunked numerous false claims surrounding Marcos’ presidential term — either having to do with not stepping down or changing the Constitution to stay in office:

items: FACT CHECK: Contrary to claim, Marcos has no plans to resign
FACT CHECK: Marcos did not say he wants another 6-year presidential term
FACT CHECK: ‘No 2028 election’ claim is ‘fake news,’ Malacañang says
FACT CHECK: Marcos statement claiming to cancel 2028 election is taken out of context

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Potato price-fixing lawsuit alleging N.B. giants are part of 'good ol' boys network' goes ahead
articles.summary: A lawsuit against major producers of frozen potato products, including two industry giants from New Brunswick, can go ahead, a U.S. judge has ruled.

image.caption: Cavendish Farms and McCain Foods, both with head offices in New Brunswick, are named in a U.S. lawsuit alleging price fixing in the frozen potato products market. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: New Brunswick
A lawsuit against major producers of frozen potato products, including two industry giants from New Brunswick, can go ahead, a U.S. judge has ruled.
Lawsuit alleges McCain, Cavendish and 2 U.S. companies conspired to raise prices
A lawsuit against major producers of frozen potato products, including two industry giants from New Brunswick, can go ahead, a U.S. judge ruled.
The class action lawsuit, launched two years ago, alleges antitrust violations by several manufacturers of frozen french fries, hash browns, tater tots and other potato products.

The four companies named in the suit — McCain Foods, Cavendish Farms, Lamb Weston and J.R. Simplot — make up a “good ol’ boys network," controlling the market in the U.S. and sharing information about pricing with each other, the suit alleges.
In a decision last month, Judge Jeffrey I. Cummings of the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois allowed most of the claims to continue.
Cavendish, which is owned by J.D Irving Ltd., has its head office in Dieppe and McCain has a head office in Florenceville-Bristol. Both Lamb Weston and J.R. Simplot are based in Idaho.
The lawsuit was filed in 2024 by Redner’s Markets, a Pennsylvania-based grocery chain.
It alleges that starting in January 2021, the four companies raised prices at “nearly identical rates around similar times” by sharing prices with each other on a program called PotatoTrack.

“Because the clients of PotatoTrack were limited to the four Producer Defendants and the United States Potato Board, the PotatoTrack reports allowed each Producer Defendant to assess critical data from the three other competitors,” the lawsuit said.

items: Alleged 'potato cartel' accused of conspiring to raise price of frozen fries, tater tots across U.S.

blocks.text: The defendants put forward a joint motion to dismiss the complaint, but Cummings mostly denied the motion.

The lawsuit said the four companies dominate the U.S. market for frozen potato products, controlling 98 per cent of it. The two Canadian companies, McCain and Cavendish, control 30 per cent and seven to eight per cent, respectively.

Any new competitors trying to enter the market would have a hard time even finding suppliers since the four major companies have long-established and exclusive relationships with potato growers, the lawsuit said.
The suit alleges that executives in the four companies develop close relationships through their membership in several potato organizations and their attendance at industry conferences.

The companies are also alleged to have knowledge about each other's business practices through co-packing arrangements in which on one manufacturer outsources part of its production to another company.
Cummings wrote that the companies didn’t make a good enough argument to have the lawsuit dismissed.
“It is well-settled that the exchange of price information among competitors is indicative of anticompetitive agreement,” Cummings wrote.
The four companies' control of most of the U.S. market is insufficient to prove a price-fixing agreement, but it makes it “more plausible” that it could happen, he said.
CBC News reached out to the four companies but did not receive a response from three of them on Thursday.
A spokesperson for J.R. Simplot said in an email that the company "is committed to competing fairly and with integrity in all markets where we operate and in compliance with applicable laws."

When the lawsuit was first brought in 2024, McCain said in a statement that it strongly disputed the allegations and would vigorously defend itself. The other three companies did not respond to requests for comment at that time.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sam Farley is a Fredericton-based reporter at CBC New Brunswick. Originally from Boston, he is a journalism graduate of the University of King's College in Halifax. He can be reached at sam.farley@cbc.ca

blocks.text: An initial interim report by the independent body investigating the crash confirms the high-speed Ave train was travelling at between 160 and 200km/h when it collided with the stationary train ahead of it.

Despite a lot of attention on leaked recordings of conversations between the operations centre and drivers affected by a signalling failure in the Urda area, the full investigation is likely to take weeks if not months. The investigators were not able to speak to some of the key witnesses so far, the interim report said.
But, as our Spain correspondent Sam Jones notes in his analysis, the effect on Spain’s politics can be more imminent given next month’s parliamentary elections.
“The crash could sap Sánchez’s recently resurgent momentum and the issue of rail safety now threatens to overshadow his attempts to defend his record and remain in the Moncloa palace.”

Elsewhere, I will be keeping an eye on France and Italy, with more protests planned in both countries as populations continue to show their frustrations with the state of education, the cost of living and other issues.

French interior minister Laurent Nuñez warned of “a very high risk” of violent disorder this weekend, as he blamed “the radicalised far-left” and the Yellow Vest movement for urging more people to attend demonstrations with “quite radical” messages.
In Italy, “massive” students protests are expected in Rome, Milan, the student movement said.
I will bring you all the latest.

And later the attention will turn to Canada, as it continues discussing its new relationship with the EU at a summit in Montreal – whether through an “associate membership” or some other form of partnership. We will hear from Mark Carney and Ursula von der Leyen.
It’s Friday, 30 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: North Korean hackers behind $6.3-B Binance crypto theft – report
articles.summary: North Korean hacking unit TraderTraitor targets Binance wallets on 10 blockchains, moving the funds out in about 20 minutes

blocks.text: CRYPTO. Bitcoin cryptocurrency representation is pictured on a keyboard in front of binary code in this illustration taken September 24, 2021.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
North Korean hacking unit TraderTraitor targets Binance wallets on 10 blockchains, moving the funds out in about 20 minutes

MANILA, Philippines – TRM Labs, an AI investigations company and blockchain analyst group, said in a report on Thursday, October 29 (October 30, Philippine time), that the theft of $6.3 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Binance could be attributed to a hacking unit from North Korea.
In a blogpost explaining its findings, TRM said the premier North Korean hacking unit TraderTraitor was behind the attack on Binance, basing the assessment on intelligence sources it has.
TraderTraitor apparently targeted Binance wallets on 10 blockchains, moving the funds out in about 20 minutes.
While Binance has been able to freeze affected assets of about $3 billion with the help of its partners, there’s no word yet on the status of the remaining $3.3 billion

blocks.caption: Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3-billion security breach

blocks.text: TraderTraitor was also behind the $1.5-billion heist of ByBit, another cryptocurrency exchange, in 2025.
TRM added that several features of the Binance attack “match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack” and an attack on the KelpDAO exchange in 2026.
TRM said the theft of Binance “is the largest crypto theft on record.”
“Even after the stablecoin freezes, the amount the attacker still holds exceeds any previous theft,” the firm added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Many Turkish 'guest workers' hit by poverty in old age
articles.summary: On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called 'guest workers' cannot live from their pensions.

image.caption: Many of the 'guest workers' worked underground in coal minesImage: Guenay Ulutuncok/akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Düsseldorf Airport is a historically symbolic location. This is where the first Turkish "guest workers," as they were called at the time in Germany, arrived 65 years ago.
At a ceremony there in in mid-September, North Rhine-Westphalia's premier, Henrik Wüst, commemorated the courage of this first generation of migrants and their contribution to Germany's prosperity.

By the time recruitment ended in 1973, some 870,000 Turkish men and women had migrated to Germany for work. They toiled in the coal mines, did piecework on assembly lines or cleaned the factory floors. Most settled in Düsseldorf, Cologne or Duisburg. "They have made our country more diverse, more open and stronger," said Wüst. However, he also stressed: "We will have reached our goal only once name, skin color and religion no longer matter."

blocks.caption: Baden-Württemberg State Premier Cem Özdemir is the most prominent German politician of Turkish descentImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Some upward mobility among migrants, but discrimination a big problem

According to Haci-Halil Uslucan, Germany is still a long way from that. Even 65 years later, he told DW, there is still a great deal of discrimination in Germany against people of Turkish descent. However, he points out that the recruitment agreement was, in the main, a success story: "We've seen success in many areas, such as education. Today, we have a large number of college graduates, and we've seen professional advancement. And successful political careers. Take Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, for example," he said.

Uslucan is a perfect example: His father came to Berlin after 1971 and worked in the textile industry. Two years later, he brought his wife and two sons to join him. Haci-Halil Uslucan earned his Ph.D. in psychology and is now a professor of Modern Turkish Studies at the University of Duisburg-Essen. One of his most recent research topics addresses the dark side of the labor recruitment agreement — an issue that affects and troubles many former so-called 'guest workers': loneliness. But it is not just loneliness that is increasingly taking its toll on some people of Turkish descent reaching retirement age.

"Studies show that poverty in old age is twice as high among migrants — between 25% and 30% compared to 12% to 14% among Germans. The disability rate and the rate of early retirement are significantly higher among migrants because the first generation did very heavy physical labor." They are also twice as likely to become unemployed ten years before reaching retirement age, says Uslucan. "In addition, their monthly income is lower, they are more likely to have had employment gaps and worked in low-wage sectors. As a result, their pensions are also low."
Three perspectives: What does German citizenship mean?
Pensions €360 lower among Turkish citizens in Germany

A special analysis by Germany's pension insurance fund (DRV) for the Mediendienst Integration, an information service for journalists on migration topics, has come up with some alarming figures: In Germany, pensioners with Turkish citizenship receive, on average, about €360 ($403) less in pension benefits than German pensioners. At the end of 2025, the figure was €890 compared to €1,250 per month. Even more troubling is that in June 2026 more than three times as many retirees with Turkish citizenship relied on top-up welfare benefits as Germans (9.3% compared to 2.7%).

Social scientist Eric Seils of the Hans Böckler Foundation in Düsseldorf told DW that many of the 'guest workers' came to Germany were not at the start of their working lives and were therefore able to contribute less to their pension fund. "But, of course, the most important reason is that they earned less in wages and had a shorter work history. The guest workers who came to Germany often went straight to factories, mines or construction sites. There, they didn't earn high hourly wages because they were often less educated than the Germans," he added.

With deindustrialization in the early 1970s and the oil crisis, many also lost their jobs. "There weren't as many good jobs available at traditional industrial companies. Those who weren't as well-educated were more likely to become unemployed than those with an education — and the same was true for Germans. And when working lives are interrupted, that naturally has an impact on retirement benefits at some point."

blocks.caption: Coal mines in the Ruhr Valley closed during deindustrialization throwing many out of work. Some are now museumsImage: Stefan Ziese/picture alliance/Zoonar

blocks.text: Few chances for migrant workers to train

Janina Söhn of the Institute for Sociological Research (SOFI) at Göttingen University has also studied the issue of poverty among older immigrants. In her view, the fact that nearly one-third of immigrants are at risk of poverty is a major problem in Germany. "This group faces even greater hardship than, for example, women in general, who already have a higher risk of poverty. And when you then look specifically at female migrants living alone, the figures are truly dire and alarming. If there were no family support, the situation would be even sorrier."

Even the opportunity to earn a few extra euros during retirement is often unavailable to many older people of Turkish origin. Either because their qualifications — which are often limited — are insufficient, or because the hard physical labor they performed when they were younger has left them physically unfit. According to figures from the German Federal Employment Agency, their employment rate is only half that of Germans (5.2% compared to 10.8%). Söhn says: "Basically, they face a whole series of disadvantages or hardships in life. That generation of guest workers was brought to Germany and then had to do the worst jobs here, whereas many Germans were able to progress through education and training." For the guest workers, on the other hand, there were no continuing education initiatives. "The people who did these tough jobs — which are always necessary for any economy — paid for it with their health."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Ombudsman suspends 2 QC brgy. execs over P22.28M unsettled disallowances, ghost projects
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has slapped a six-month preventive suspension against Quezon City Quirino 3B (Claro) Punong Barangay Ronald Tagle and Barangay Treasurer Richelle Ann Santillan over…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 4:12pm

The Office of the Ombudsman has slapped a six-month preventive suspension against Quezon City Quirino 3B (Claro) Punong Barangay Ronald Tagle and Barangay Treasurer Richelle Ann Santillan over alleged unsettled audit disallowances and non-existent projects.

In a five-page order, the Ombudsman found that the evidence of guilt against the respondents was strong, citing Commission on Audit (COA) findings which showed non-submission of required supporting documents, as well as irregularities in the utilization, documentation, and processing of barangay funds, including non-submission of supporting documents for such fund utilization.
“Tagle, in conspiracy with Santillan, withdrew the savings of Barangay Quirino 3B (Claro) from 2018 to 2023 for non-existent or ghost projects,” the order read.
Specifically, the Ombudsman said that P1.4 million worth of procurement transactions in 2017 and 2018 were unsupported by complete documentation.
The Ombudsman also cited the following undocumented disbursements under the watch of the respondents:

items: P15.9 million in 2020
P23.9 million in 2021
P17.64 million in 2022 and
P17.88 million in 2023

blocks.text: Further the Ombudsman said that Tagle and Santillan authorized the release of P22.7 million of public funds without the required disbursement vouchers, resulting in COA's issuance of notices of disallowance.

“Respondents' administrative violation appears to be supported by evidence. The evidence on record shows that the guilt of respondents is strong, the charges against them involve Grave Misconduct, and Gross Neglect of Duty,” the Ombudsman said.
"The charges against them involved offenses that may warrant removal from service, and their continued stay in office could prejudice the administrative proceedings," the order added.
The complaint against the barangay officials was filed by the Office of the Ombudsman’s Field Investigation Office.

The anti-graft body tasked Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte to immediately implement the preventive suspension and inform the Office of the Ombudsman of the action taken within three days of receipt of the order.

Sought for comment, Tagle and Santillan told GMA News Online via phone call that they are continuously addressing the COA findings and have filed a motion for reconsideration before the Ombudsman on October 30. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: 'You can't just get out': How 2 boys were recruited into the drug trade at the age of 12
articles.byline: Aliyah Marko-Omene, Shelley Ayres, Mark Kelley, Danielle Reid

image.caption: Teen boys across Canada are being lured to work on the front lines of a lucrative and dangerous drug trade in remote communities, CBC's the fifth estate has found. (Shelley Ayres/CBC)

blocks.text: Kai was 12 years old when he began to warn his mother he might not make it home.
"[If] I don't make it home by four o'clock, just know that I got snatched and somebody put me in their car and kidnapped me," he would tell her.

His mother, whom CBC's the fifth estate is calling Aria for her protection, moved her family to another city when Kai was a boy to disconnect from his father, who had a criminal past and street associations.
She enrolled Kai, whose name has also been changed for his protection, in community centres and drop-in spaces in Winnipeg to keep him busy and away from trouble
But Aria believes those spaces exposed her son to people who would exploit him.

items: Watch the full documentary, "Missing Boys: Lured into Danger," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: She believes some staff abused their positions, allowing gang members to manipulate her son and coerce him into the drug trade — sending him thousands of kilometres away from home.

Fifth estate host Mark Kelley, left, sits down with a boy who was recruited by a gang when he was 12. He says he has been sent out of town to sell drugs more times than he can count. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Kai said men in their 20s and 30s presented themselves as people he could trust.
"People call it grooming, people call it using. There's many words for it, but it's just being taken advantage of because you're innocent," Kai said.

For the last two years, the fifth estate has investigated the disappearances of young Black boys from the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) who are groomed and lured into drug trafficking networks in Ontario cities as far away as Sarnia and Thunder Bay, and sent further north into Indigenous communities like Ginoogaming, a First Nation.

items: How gangs lure Black boys to northern Ontario 'trap houses'

blocks.text: Now, the fifth estate has heard directly from boys who live this dangerous life and say they were sent across the country to sell drugs, revealing a network that reaches even farther.

We now know of this activity taking boys as young as 12 as far west as British Columbia, as far north as Yellowknife and as far east as Halifax — places where drugs are sold at exponentially higher prices — up to 10 times the price in some cases.
The business of going OT
In an interview with CBC's the fifth estate, Kai recounts his first trip out of town, also known as “going OT,” when he was 12.
"You don't know what's in those bags. You don't know what you're delivering for people … you just think, 'I'm helping the older guy, because I want to be cool like him,'" he said.
Kai said the older men picked him up, told him where he would stay and expected him to sell drugs. He was left in a remote community eight hours north of his home in Winnipeg.
LISTEN: The Missing Boys: When It All Went Wrong
Kai said he did not fully understand what he was getting into. He had to figure it out in a place where he did not know anyone and his family was out of reach.
"You're not telling family members," he said. "Because not only do they not know where you are, you don't know where you are."
The first trip taught him more about what he calls the rules of "the game," where the three outcomes are freedom, jail or death.
And he says he was forced to gamble for the gangs.
"You can't just get out ... whoever sent you there is expecting you to come back with a prize," Kai said. "And if you don't come back with anything … God forbid something happens to you."
Now 14, Kai has made more trips out of town than he can count.
On the front line of the drug trade
Jamal, another teenager whose name has been changed for his safety, started going OT at 12. He had been away from home for more than a week and his mom reported him missing.
The now-18-year-old who lives in the Toronto area said he has been sent to communities in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.
Jamal's farthest trip took him to Yellowknife. He was even convinced to pay his own way.

Like Kai, Jamal said it was in Grade 7 when he was first approached to work for a gang. His family had spent a year bouncing between houses and he grew close to older people in his neighbourhood who were often around his cousins.
"I always just had the respect and looked at them like an older role model," he said.
Jamal said those role models could offer him an escape from the instability at home.

items: Searching for Ontario’s missing Black boys
Calls to stem violence in northern First Nations as Ginoogaming man’s family mourns shooting death

blocks.text: "If things were stable at home, I wouldn't really have a reason to go outside," he said.
Jamal said the adults he worked for were selling drugs bought internationally — and worked with cartels.

Then Jamal tells the fifth estate how the boys cross the country — a key piece of information — as many families are baffled as to how their boys are boarding planes and driving to remote locations when they are too young to have a driver's licence and don't have identification.
Jamal said fake names and identification are provided for them.
"It doesn't even matter who you are, how young you are. You can go anywhere in Canada," he said. "It's actually quite easy."
The adults behind the operation
The fifth estate previously found adult traffickers use the boys as disposable mules and legal shields that often take the fall when police make drug busts.

A 2026 federal Justice Department report found that the proportion of Black youth in correctional supervision in Nova Scotia, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia remained at around 12 to 13 per cent from 2019 to 2024. That's almost two times more than their combined share of the population for that age group, across all four provinces.

Black boys often face well-known socio-economic challenges including high unemployment, and bias within justice and educational systems that can make them more vulnerable to the pull of organized crime.
"Many of these youth[s] are exploited … they're seen as disposable to the people who are running these networks," said Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski.

Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski tells the fifth estate the drugs supplied by gangs have been linked to international cartels. Young boys are often used for street-level dealing so gang members don't have to expose themselves to violence or being arrested. (Oliver Walters/CBC)
In May, Ewatski led a team involved in what police called Manitoba's largest drug bust. Investigators seized 525 kilograms of cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl in Winnipeg.
Those arrested included people associated with Canada's highest ranks of organized crime including the Hells Angels, Wolfpack Alliance and a Mexican cartel.
"Most of the drugs of cocaine and methamphetamine will come from Mexico up to the U.S. and into Canada," Ewatski said.
He described a sophisticated network where multiple drug trafficking organizations are working together to move drugs into remote communities.
He says it's associates of these international criminal networks who are recruiting and using boys.
Ewatski said boys are used for street-level dealing and to work in stash houses. He said they often don't know who they are working for.
"These kids are used so [those running the networks] don't have to expose themselves to being arrested or being shot."
Leaving a gang can be just as dangerous. Ewatski said some boys become trapped by debts they are told they owe their recruiters.
“If they're out, they're going to be out in a violent way," he said. "Possibly even dead."
Denny Heathen, a reformed gang member, now counsels youth and leads prayer circles in his community of Prince Albert, Sask. (Shelley Ayres/CBC)

Denny Heathen spent much of his 20s working for a gang in Prince Albert, Sask. He said some recruiters targeted boys between 15 to 18 and told us that the boys who were targeted had a look of desperation.
"They wanted purpose," Heathen said.
Recruiters offered attention, money and the promise of protection, presenting themselves as brothers or older mentors.
"These are puppets," he said. "You just got to make them feel like they're appreciated, like they are going to be taken care of."
What it takes to get out of a gang
Kai remembers the grooming process well.
“You're a little kid in a community centre trying to play basketball and then you see these guys … walking around with the large prize in their hand."
The prize was money — an amount that felt impossible to a boy too young to get his first job.
During his interview with the fifth estate, Kai pulled out a thick stack of $100 bills to demonstrate how quickly money could influence a boy to sell drugs.
"All it takes is this and you're influenced."
He said the amounts involved can be enormous in First Nations communities where an oxycodone pill can sell for $200.
"That substance that is being put in these boys' pockets and these boys' hands to go deal over the province … people will do anything for."
The boy who never came home
On March 27, 2025, Jay'siiah Webb-Long walked out of his family's home in Brampton, Ont., carrying a single duffel bag that appeared nearly empty.

Doorbell camera footage provided by the family to the fifth estate shows the 15-year-old placing a single box in the recycling bin on his front porch, scanning the street before disappearing out of frame.
His story made national headlines.
Jay'siiah Webb-Long, 15, was last seen outside his home in Brampton, Ont. on March 27, 2025. (Saskatchewan RCMP)
"Somebody had sent me photos after his disappearance," said Shenice Long, his mother.
"She had sent photos of him holding stacks of money. So, at that point, I said, 'OK, somebody has sent him far out … to make money.'"
Long said she remained in contact with her son for weeks after he left home. But he would not tell her where he was.

Jay'siiah's family told the fifth estate they are frustrated with action from Peel Regional Police and the RCMP in Saskatchewan, citing for example that it took Peel police eight weeks to alert the public that Jay'siiah was missing.

Long said police used a phone number she never had for her son to trace his location to Pelican Narrows, Sask., a northern community about 3,000 kilometres from his home in Brampton. This number only surfaced when the public alert came out and a young woman came forward.
"I heard of Saskatchewan, but … I don't have family there. I don't know anyone there," Long said.
In July 2025, Saskatchewan RCMP took over the file as a homicide investigation. They didn't alert the public of this shift until September 2025.
Police told the family a search was delayed by winter weather. In the spring, investigators told the family they planned to search near Pelican Narrows — led with cadaver dogs.
Pelican Narrows, Sask., a community of about 4,000 and located about 500 kilometres north of Saskatoon, is part of the Peter Ballantyne Cree Nation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
On May 13, human remains were found near a sewage lagoon just outside the community. An autopsy confirmed two days later that the remains belonged to Webb-Long.
RCMP believe his death was a homicide. The investigation is ongoing and no charges have been laid in connection with his death.
Missing — and not always reported

In 2024, 322 male youth were reported missing to Toronto police. Statistics Canada data shows Black boys account for almost half of those missing, despite representing less than 10 per cent of the city's population of that age group.

The fifth estate has found not every family reports their youth missing. In the case of Jay'siiah Webb-Long, his mother didn't file a formal report until three weeks after he had left home. She told the fifth estate she had called Peel Regional Police after 48 hours but they dissuaded her because she was still in contact with him.

"One youth missing is too [many]," said Christene Lewis, who is a violence intervention specialist and works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas. She supports many families who have youth that go missing and go "OT." It's a life she knows because she lived it.
"I come from the gang culture," Lewis said. "I come from feeling isolated, I've come from feeling like the streets were more loyal to me than my own family was."
Christene Lewis, a violence intervention specialist, works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas who have youth who go missing. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Lewis said some parents hesitate reporting their child missing because they fear their kids will be treated as runaways rather than young people at risk. Others feel shame and embarrassment.
Lewis said there is also a breakdown of trust between marginalized communities and police.
"They don't feel like the police even care."
Lewis's advice to parents: Always report a missing kid and keep following up.
"If they didn't hear you the first day, call the next day," she said. "Don't give up."
A message for parents of missing kids
Aria remembers when it first became clear her son had gone to a First Nations community to sell drugs.
"He was telling stories like he came back from camp," she said.
He would leave home sporadically, returning home with designer clothing and money.
Aria said she has also had the windows of her home shot at three times.
Now, when Kai goes missing, she reports him and collects evidence that might help police locate him.
"This is not something you make peace with," she said. "This is something that's wrong."
'Nobody's just going to let you go'
Jamal said the people who recruited him continue to contact him and tell him he owes them money.
''They're going to keep texting you, telling you that they got this opportunity … nobody's just going to let you just go."
Kai has also tried to leave. He spent the summer away at camp and returned determined to get out of gang life.
"Now that I realize what kind of hell on earth is like … I never want to go back there," he told the fifth estate in August.
But Aria said the messages continued.
She found text messages about Kai from a sibling that read: "I will not be returning your little bro" and "he's my slave.”
She believes the messages are proof her son is being trafficked.
Aria, a Winnipeg mother whose name has been changed for protection, worries gangs will never loosen their grip on her son. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Kai left home again the night before he was set to start Grade 10. He returned home and left again several times.
Aria fears that even if Kai manages to break free from the gangs, they will continue to chase and manipulate him, tempting him with money and a sense of belonging.
Kai is facing drug trafficking charges.
"This monster exists and it's going to exist on his path as a young man, as an adult," Aria said. "I don't think that this monster ever goes away."
